pistons.headline: Pistons at Hawks final score: Detroit outscored by 21 in the fourth, lose 107-97
pistons.body:
ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 22: Nickeil Alexander-Walker #7 of the Atlanta Hawks reacts after hitting a three-point basket against the Detroit Pistons during the first quarter at State Farm Arena on November 22, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images

That was an unbelievable collapse by Detroit, and quite possibly the worst game of Cade Cunningham’s career.

The Pistons went into the fourth quarter with an 85-74 lead. They outscored the Hawks by 10 in the third quarter, and ESPN had Detroit at a 90% chance to win the game when the final frame started.

That went downhill quickly as the Hawks went on an 18-0 run to open the fourth quarter. The Pistons didn’t score their first points until Isaiah Joe hit a corner three with 4:52 left in the game. Detroit’s offense stalled, the ball wasn’t moving, and for whatever reason, Cade Cunningham and Daniss Jenkins took it upon themselves to try to iso Dyson Daniels and Lu Dort. As you can tell, it didn’t work.

Detroit shot better from the field, the three-point line, and the free-throw line. They even scored more points in the paint than the Hawks, but couldn’t manage to grab a rebound. Atlanta grabbed 19 more rebounds than Detroit and outrebounded the Pistons on the offensive glass 24-8. If there was ever a game that showed Detroit needed Jalen Duren back ASAP, this was it.

Atlanta had 10 more fastbreak points than Detroit, and second-chance points went in a massive favor of the Hawks to the tune of 27-6. Detroit’s rebounding was horrendous – outside of Ausar Thompson’s 11 boards, John Collins was second on the team with six.

Cade Cunningham scored in single digits for the first time all season with five points while shooting 2-for-9 from the field. He also added four rebounds and 15 assists in what is surely one of the weirdest stat lines of his career. Kevin Huerter was a -28 on the floor while shooting 1-for-8 for a measly two points.

Oddly enough, it was Isaiah Joe who led the team in scoring with 19 points on 15 attempts. Joe was +11 tonight and knocked down three threes. John Collins and Ausar Thompson each had 18 points. Collins made four threes, and Ausar added five assists. Paul Reed had 16 points off the bench, and Daniss Jenkins had 11.

In what should’ve been a victory tonight in Atlanta, Detroit blew their double-digit lead and deserved to lose this game. That was one of the worst fourth quarter performances I’ve ever watched, and it looked like a middle school team that couldn’t grab a rebound in a scrimmage against the high school varsity.

Please, Jalen Duren, come back soon.

Detroit moves to 10-6 on the year and will now travel to Orlando to take on the Magic on Tuesday night. Let’s hope this Pistons team has a short memory and burns tonight’s fourth quarter tape.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Raptors final score: Cade vs. Scottie battle goes to Raps
pistons.body:
[DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 20: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons plays defense on Scottie Barnes #4 of the Toronto Raptors during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on November 20, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Chris Schwegler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Two former teammates and two Eastern Conference teams traded body blows all night. A Cade Cunningham 3-pointer to put the Pistons up 102-101 with 20 seconds left was answered by a Scottie Barnes driving layup over two defenders to give the Raptors the lead they would not relinquish. When a Kevin Huerter three came up short as the buzzer sounded, it was decided. Raptors 105-102.

Cunningham led Detroit with 23 points and nine assists, but he was outshined on this night by his former Montverde teammate Barnes, who led all scorers with 29 points and hit his first nine shots of the night.

While it was appointment television watching the two top players on each team matched up with each other, the rest of the game was pretty much a horror show for the Pistons. Distilling why the Pistons dropped this game will sound very familiar to Pistons fans — not owning the paint.

Detroit surrendered 54 points inside to Toronto and gave up crucial offensive rebounds late. It’s one thing to see Barnes put a great game on you, but Detroit was owned inside by rookie Allen Graves making his first start of the season. He scored 20 points, had 10 rebounds, including four on the offensive end. Detroit simply had no answer for him. Certainly not John Collins.

The overmatched emergency starting center struggled again in just under 20 minutes of action. He was just 1-of-4 from the floor for three points and six rebounds. The return of Isaiah Joe from injury isn’t looking very different from when he was playing early in the season — he’s still struggling to find his shot. Joe was 1-of-6 from deep tonight. Getting those kinds of performances from your two highest-profile offseason acquisitions is not the recipe for winning basketball.

The other major issue tonight is that you were facing one of the worst-shooting offenses in the NBA and on this night, they could not miss. Some of that had to do with Detroit’s occasionally passive defense. But tonight, the Raptors players were just collectively on one. We already covered how hot Barnes was, especially early, but the sweet shooting was up and down the roster.

The rookie Graves was 6-of-9, Jakob Poeltl was 5-of-7, and Immanuel Quickly was 6-of-10. Collectively, Toronto shot 67% inside the arc tonight. Again, I’m going to point to the big black hole in the middle of Detroit’s lineup. A combination of John Collins and Paul Reed as your only big men is just not going to get it done in the NBA. The Pistons need Jalen Duren to come back desperately.

The loss to the Raptors drops the Pistons to 1-1 in NBA Cup play, but then again, I refuse to care about the NBA Cup. Detroit now goes on a mini road trip to Atlanta on Sunday and Orlando on Tuesday before enjoying seven of the next eight games at home.

The Toronto Raptors are scuffling in the first leg of the NBA season, but there is certainly a lot of talent there. Yes, Kawhi Leonard is absent with news of managing knee pain and swelling that surely puts a shiver up the spine of every Toronto fan. But they also still have Scottie Barnes, and he is delivering the young star goods as advertised. He is averaging 23.8 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 4.7 assists a night. On certain nights, he looks like the young superstar that represents his clearly attainable ceiling. On other nights, he and his team’s offense struggle and can’t seem to get unstuck from the mud. He’s doing a lot of things, but he isn’t doing it as efficiently or consistently as you’d like.

The real problems with the Raptors, though, lie elsewhere. Nobody can seemingly hit a three. RJ Barrett is getting to the line five times a game and hitting just 60% from the charity stripe. Collin Murray-Boyles has regressed, and Jakob Poeltl’s game has fallen off a cliff. It feels like if you solve Scottie, it helps you solve Barrett and Immanuel Quickley, and therefore, you solve the Raptors. Toronto has dropped six straight, and will be without the services of Barrett tonight.

Watching an Ausar Thompson and Scottie Barnes matchup could be electric. Barnes doesn’t have the defensive chops Ausar does, and Ausar doesn’t have the offensive versatility, but both could be liable to pull off a triple-double tonight. Cade Cunningham is also expected back tonight after sitting out Detroit’s win against the New Orleans Pelicans. Duncan Robinson and Ron Holland are out, and doubtful, respectively.

pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - OCTOBER 16: Isaiah Joe #17 of the Detroit Pistons shoots the ball during the game against the Toronto Raptors on October 16, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. Early season Fridays = NBA Cup day! The Detroit Pistons can climb to 2-0 in group play with a win over the worse-than-expected Toronto Raptors (1-1 in group play). The NBA thought this would’ve been a big game, handing out the Prime Video first game slot, but injuries, injuries, injuries.

Ron Holland, Duncan Robinson, and Jalen Duren are out again, but Cade Cunningham is expected to play. Injuries have slowed down the Raptors a ton.

RJ Barrett and Collin Murray-Boyles won’t suit up in Detroit. Kawhi Leonard remains out. His absence is the main source of Toronto’s struggle, but I still expected more.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 7:30 PM ET

Watch: Prime Video

Odds: Pistons (-6.5)

The Raptors are still live even though they should be better. That said, Detroit isn’t a team that takes opponents lightly because of who’s in or out. The Pistons play the same brand of ball regardless of who’s out there on either side.

Wednesday’s 122-109 win over the New Orleans Pelicans tripled down on that point. Even a shorthanded Pistons squad without Cade manages to find a way.

Daniss Jenkins. Javonte Green. Ausar Thompson with the ball. Paul Reed with extended minutes — trustworthy things.

We got Isaiah Joe back in the lineup in that one! One of the marquee signings of Detroit’s offseason let it fly. Joe went 3-for-5 from range and put it on the floor, aiding Detroit’s flow. Bball Paul said Joe had more in his game during media day. Paul knows ball.

What do you know, it's Isaiah Joe

-Pistons able to flow into early offense with nothing there on initial push. DHO and now Joe gets a flare with an empty side
-Huerter cuts backdoor, pindown for Joe with an empty side. Turns the corner and the lob is there. pic.twitter.com/LZ8FQlRRAH
— Steve Jones (@stevejones20) November 19, 2026

The ability to leverage your shooting with live dribble decisions is an invaluable skill come playoff time. Love seeing Joe back out there, and more of that would be cool.

John Collins was on a heater (4-6 on 3s). He should get six 3s up every night with the room he has to fire. Collins will be matched up with Jakob Poeltl tonight. Poeltl is arguably the biggest hacker in the league. His 5.6 foul percentage ranks in the fourth percentile among bigs.

A lot of those Cade drives should end with trips to the charity stripe. Cade’s .37 FTr is a career high. He’s getting the calls and shooting ~86 percent at the line. That works. Cade is also putting together a strong All-Defense case, being a big-time contributor on the sixth-best defense.

Per Stathead, only Cade, Nikola Jokić, Matisse Thybulle, Scottie Barnes, and Caleb Wilson are averaging at least 0.9 blocks and 1.4 steals. Cade is doing this without fouling. He’s leveling up even more on that end.

Barnes recently declared himself the best defender in the world. I have no problem with that. He is up there. He’s a legit 1-5 defender. Anybody that good at something should feel they’re the best. That confidence got them where they are.

Barnes is Barnes, but I thought Toronto would have a more intimidating team defense. Cleaning The Glass ranks them 17th overall and 19th over the past two weeks + they are on a six-game losing streak.

The injury bug cannot be ignored, but I thought Toronto would be immune to long stretches of defensive lapses because of their suffocating gap principles.

Those principles still force turnovers at a frightening rate (2nd), but they haven’t dug in and clamped down like last year’s Raptors team. They’re still feisty enough to muddy up a game, but I expected more.

Toronto’s off-the-bounce creation takes a big blow with no Kawhi and Barrett. Barnes has more shot-making responsibilities this season. His 23.8 points per game are a career high. Immanuel Quickley will get them up. Catching fire vs. Ausar and the Pistons’ defense isn’t easy, but Toronto is looking to Quickley to provide immediate offense.

Jamison Battle is one of Toronto’s consistent snipers. He’s not a shooter you can disregard and is coming off a 19-point, 5-for-10 from 3 game. Ja’Kobe Walter can shoot it too and is quietly turning into a dependable heavy-minute wing.

With a win, Detroit could be in first or second in the East Group A division. The Orlando Magic (2-0) take on the struggling Brooklyn Nets (0-1) tonight. Should Orlando snag a win, they stay atop the group.

One game and one week at a time for Detroit in this tournament. They smacked around the Nets in their first cup game and look to do the same against the Raptors.

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (10-4): Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

Toronto Raptors (5-10): Immanuel Quickley, Ja’Kobe Walter, Jamison Battle, Scottie Barnes, Jakob Poeltl

Question of the Day

The New York Knicks won the NBA Cup tourney and the real thing last year. Did that add any validity to the tournament?

pistons.body:
NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 18: Paul Reed #7 of the Detroit Pistons dunks in front of Karlo Matković #17 of the New Orleans Pelicans during the first half of a game at Smoothie King Center on November 18, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With as long as Detroit’s injury report has been recently, it got a little longer with Cade Cunningham as a late addition tonight. After the Pistons’ big win against San Antonio last night, it’s no surprise Deuce got some rest on the second night of a back-to-back.

JB Bickerstaff, with his shorthanded roster, rolled out the unusual starting lineup of Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Javonte Green, Ausar Thompson, and John Collins. This would’ve been a great game for Ebuka Okorie to get some minutes, but he hurt his hip with the Motor City Cruise just the other day.

This meant Detroit’s key bench pieces were Paul Reed, Chaz Lanier, and Elijah Harkless. Even Tolu Smith saw some spot minutes when Collins and Reed both needed rest. Luckily, Isaiah Joe made his return to the lineup tonight after missing the last several games. Despite having to play guys from the end of the bench and on two-way spots, Detroit didn’t struggle against New Orleans.

Remember that unusual starting lineup for Detroit? Well, every single one of them finished in double digits. Jenkins, Green, and Collins all made at least three three-pointers. Jenkins, Thompson, and Huerter all had at least four assists, though Huerter had seven and DJ added nine.

Both Lanier and Joe made three three-pointers off the bench. Reed was the key sixth man once again, though that’s not all that peculiar nowadays. Harkless played his most minutes so far this season and did a great job sharing the rock with four assists.

In a game without their star player, this was another complete team win. There’s no doubt the depth on this team is one of the best in the league, and Detroit had seven different players score in double digits. Your Detroit Pistons are now 10-4 on the year.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Pelicans preview:  Closing out the road trip in New Orleans
pistons.body:
The Pistons have played a lot of road games so far this season.  They have also played less games than a lot of other teams because of that.  Last night’s game against the San Antonio Spurs was probably their toughest test of the season so far, and they passed it with flying colors.

The Spurs were in the midst of a 12 game winning streak and playing at home against a Pistons team down 4 players who were in their opening night rotation.  Despite that, they went into San Antonio and imposed their will and came out on top.

Now, they head to New Orleans to close out this 4-game road trip against a Pelicans team that has struggled this season.  After a game like last night, these are the exact kind of games that can be a bit of a trap, so hopefully the Pistons come out ready to play and close out this road trip with a 3-1 record.

The Pistons are still set to be short-handed, but as they proved last night, that doesn’t matter to this team.

Game Vitals

Where:  Smoothie King Center in New Orleans, LA
When:  Wednesday, November 18 at 8 pm EST
Watch:  Scripps Sports Network
Odds:  Pistons (-7.5)

Analysis

I mentioned the Pistons injuries above, as they are expected to once again be without Isaiah Joe, Duncan Robinson, Taurean Prince, Ron Holland, and Jalen Duren.  However, New Orleans is also without a slew of rotation players like Benedict Mathurin, Trey Murphy III, and Dejounte Murray.  The biggest difference is the Pistons have one of the deepest rosters in the league to overcome missing some key players while the Pelicans have a less talented roster.

None of that is to say that this game will be easy, but after a hard-fought battle against the Spurs last night, it will be nice to not have to deal with an imposing force like Victor Wembanyama again.

The Pistons depth was put to the test against the Spurs and the Pistons proved why they are one of the best teams in the Eastern Conference by coming out on top.  Of course, it was led by great 2-way performances by Cade Cunningham and Ausar Thompson, but that is to be expected of the Pistons two stars.

The Pelicans don’t present that same size-related issues the Pistons have had to deal with in their last few games, which is lucky for them.  The Pelicans do have a couple of players capable of taking over a game, like Jordan Poole and Zion Williamson, so it is important that the Pistons stay disciplined on defense, but Zion Williamson at least doesn’t tower over players like Ausar Thompson, who has had to take on more big matchups with the Pistons opting to start John Collins at center.

The Collins at center lineup has had a bit of diminishing returns lately as he has struggled to deal with size and rebounding, but it has allowed the Pistons to start Daniss Jenkins, who has been on a heater lately.  He had 25 points, 5 rebounds, and 5 assists last night against the Spurs and a couple of clutch shots.  He also had 21 and 22 points in back-to-back games against the Wizards after a 31 point game against the Lakers.  The Pistons will have a tough decision to make when Jalen Duren returns as they probably should continue to start Jenkins, but Duren doesn’t bring the same level of spacing as John Collins does and John Collins was signed to complement Jalen Duren at the four.

But, those are the good problems to have when you have a team as deep as the Pistons.

Another player to watch for the Pelicans is Jeremiah Fears, who had a triple-double in the Pelicans’ dismantling of the Golden State Warriors on Monday.  He is starting to put things together and develop into their future at point guard right at a time when Dejounte Murray has requested a trade.  Say what you want about the process in how the Pelicans have drafted and acquired picks in the last couple seasons, but they at least appear to have hit on Fears.

Another reclamation project they have hit on is former Piston, Saddiq Bey.  He earned an extension in the offseason after putting together a pretty solid season last year after recovering from the torn ACL he suffered a couple years ago.  As Pistons fans know, Bey is capable of getting hot, so he is another player they will have to look out for.

Overall, this shouldn’t be too difficult of a matchup for the Pistons, but after the emotions of a hard-fought battle last night, I would not be shocked to see a slow start out of the Pistons.  But, even with the injured players, the Pistons are the more talented team and should be able to win this game.

Lineups

Detroit Pistons (9-4):  Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Heurter, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

New Orleans Pelicans (5-10):  Jeremiah Fears, Herb Jones, Saddiq Bey, Zion Williamson, Yves Missi

The Detroit Lions (8-2) are back home in Week 12 and preparing to host the Chicago Bears (8-2) for their annual Thanksgiving Day game. With the Lions on a short week, they’ve elected to hold a walkthrough on Monday.

A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based on how the player would have participated in a traditional practice. So, with that in mind, let’s look at Monday’s injury report and get you up to date on what we know.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded.

Injured list updates

RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back, IR) — expected to be out until December

C Cade Mays (ankle, IR) — eligible to return to practice in Week 15

OL Giovanni Manu (undisclosed, NFI)

OL Ben Bartch (foot, IR)

LB Devin White (forearm, IR)

LB Jack Campbell (neck, IR)

S Thomas Harper (ankle, IR)

Estimated no practice

DT Skyler Gill-Howard (knee) — New injury

EDGE DJ Wonnum (back) — New Injury

S Chuck Clark (hamstring) — New injury

CB Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder) — Downgraded from limited

Gill-Howard appeared to suffer a leg injury late in Sunday’s game and was seen walking gingerly in the locker room, bypassing interviews to get treatment from trainers. On a short week, there is some concern for his ability to recover in time to play against the Bears, but it’s too early to make any sweeping decisions.

Wonnum played nearly three-quarters of defensive snaps on Sunday, while Clark played every snap against the Bucs, right on par with both ot thier usual workloads. Neither appeared to be affected by their injuries, so it’s possible they popped up after the game, and the Lions are being proactive. We should get updates from coach Dan Campbell at his press conference tomorrow.

Rakestraw was limited all week with a shoulder injury and was declared inactive at game time. With the Lions going light at corner, it’s unclear whether he was inactive because of his injury, a coaching decision, or a combination of both. That said, starting the week by not practicing isn’t a great sign.

Estimated limited practice

TE Sam LaPorta (ankle) — New injury

Like Wonnum and Clark, LaPorta played his traditional number of snaps and didn’t appear to be limited by injury on Sunday. However, his being estimated to have been limited is a positive sign that he has a real chance to play on Thursday. Hopefully, we will get an update on his status on Tuesday from Campbell.

Estimated full practice

CB D.J. Reed (hip) — Upgraded

CB Khalil Dorsey (wrist) — New Injury

Reed took in limited practices all last week, was listed as questionable, but did not play against the Bucs. This wasn’t surprising, as Reed said earlier in the week he planned to take his recovery slow. He’s been consistently making encouraging progress, so he could be close to playing as soon as Thursday, but his status could end up being a game-time decision again.

Dorsey was limited in practices last week with an ankle injury, but managed to play in the game, and is no longer listed as having an ankle injury. Unfortunately, Dorsey appeared to injure his wrist punching at the football and was forced out of the game for testing. On a positive note, Dorsey was able to return for special teams reps and is estimated to have practiced in full, meaning he’s in a decent spot to stay in the mix on Thursday.

RB Sione Vaki (ankle)

DL Tyler Lacy (shoulder)

LB Joe Bachie (knee)

lions.headline: Dan Campbell provides promising update after Kerby Joseph’s 1st game back
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 22: Kerby Joseph #31 of the Detroit Lions takes the field during player introductions before the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field on November 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Last week, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said the real tell about Kerby Joseph’s return to the lineup will be how he feels after the game. The knee injury that held him out for over a year wasn’t going to be as much of a problem on Sunday as it may be after playing on it for three hours.

But Campbell provided some great news on Monday. The Lions coach said Joseph came out of Sunday’s win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with no cause for concern the day after.

“I think pretty good here. There’s no red flags,” Campbell said. “So that’s a good sign.”

Joseph played 46 defensive snaps on Sunday as part of Detroit’s three-safety looks vs. the Bucs. He regularly manned the deep section of the field, while Brian Branch dropped down to nickel, and veteran Chuck Clark roamed the entirety of the field. While Joseph finished with just two tackles, Campbell said there were ups and downs to his afternoon.

“He’ll be better for those reps, just like Branch was, to get his first reps of the season,” Campbell said. “So, I thought he did some good things. There are things that he’s going to only just get better at now that he’s been out there. I thought it was pretty good. When you’re able to get he and BB on the field and you’ve got Chuck out there, it’s a pretty good unit.”

After the game, Joseph told reporters he felt no discomfort in his knee for the entirety of the game.

“Every time I come out here, I feel like myself,” Joseph said. “I don’t know why you keep asking that. I’m going to always be me. I’m going to forever be me.”

At this point, it appears Joseph is on track to play on a short week against the Chicago Bears, but we’ll know more when the team drops their first injury report of the week on Monday. Detroit is only expected to conduct walkthroughs this week, so participation levels will be estimated.

lions.headline: The Lions made the Bucs’ top-rated defense look fraudulent in Week 11 win
lions.body: The Detroit Lions put together a dominant offensive performance against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 11. Detroit's explosive offense continues to show why the Lions are among the NFL's most dangerous teams heading into the final stretch of the season.

lions.headline: The Detroit Lions are still no one’s favorites because of September
lions.body:
Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images | Getty Images

For the Detroit Lions, a six-game winning streak, a high-powered offense, and a defense that’s decidedly turned things around since Week 5 isn’t enough to earn consideration from the media as one of the premier teams in the NFL. Despite being atop the NFC North, the Lions aren’t even the team to beat in their own division.

How the Lions continue to fly under the radar on a national level is, on one hand, expected. They can’t outplay their geography. They don’t play in New York or California or Illinois, states home to the three biggest sports media markets in the country. They’re not “America’s Team” or the up-and-comers they were ahead of the 2023 season. The pillars of their team remain unchanged from the beginning of a run that includes three of four seasons where the Lions have started the season 8-2 or better—something the franchise had never done in the 60 seasons prior. No matter what they accomplish, preconceptions plague this team.

They’re still led by the same Jared Goff everyone decided was the NFL’s Charlie-in-the-Box—the gatekeeper for the Island of Misfit Toys. Remember Charlie from Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer? He lives on the Island of Misfit Toys because he’s named “Charlie” instead of “Jack,” believing his name is “all wrong” and that no child would ever want a second-rate Charlie-in-the-Box.

So sure, Jared looks and acts just as good as the real thing, but his name isn’t Joe or Josh, the names of quarterbacks everyone else fawns over in MVP discussions. The teams of Joe and Josh are being carried by elite quarterback play, and their teams’ mediocre defenses be damned: they’re in firm control of their respective divisions.

As for the Lions defense, that’s what’s going to sink their ship this season, just as it did in 2024 when the team went 15-2 and lost to the Washington Commanders in the Divisional Round. According to the pundits, this defense is still the same turnstile it was during the first month of the season, except now its without two of their top defenders in Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson—how could Detroit possibly be considered a top-10 team? In fact, their defensive core will not play a single game together this season, so consider their Super Bowl window shattered.

Mind you, we all live in our own echo chambers, seeds planted on a screen where our algorithms grow around us into any shape we encourage it to take: it’s an environment as real as the world. It becomes the truth, it is the truth. So while we play part in creating these environments, it doesn’t excuse these takes as any less misinformed than they actually are. It’s what makes finding the right coverage for football—or anything, really—all that more difficult. Digital literacy is the single most useful tool in protecting our most important currency in today’s day and age: our attention.

If you’re still paying attention, the Lions defense ranks 12th in EPA/play and eighth in success rate since Week 5 per SumerSports. The run defense ranks first in EPA/rush and third in success rate against the run. Their pass defense has creeped its way toward becoming an above-average unit since the return of Brian Branch in Week 7: 12th in EPA/pass and ninth in success rate against the pass. When you put that unit opposite of an offense that ranks sixth in EPA/play and third in success rate this season—fifth in EPA/play and sixth in success rate since Week 5—you can see why they’ve rattled off six wins in a row.

Yet, somehow, it feels like it could all be for naught if Ben Johnson and the Chicago Bears leave Ford Field with a win on Thursday. Dan Campbell will make no excuses for his team if they can’t pull off their third win in the past 11 days, but you can count on the talking heads to deem the Bears as the crown jewel of the NFC North, if not the entire conference. But if the Lions, the current underdogs for this Thanksgiving Day showdown, beat the Bears, rest assured, you can count on some special pleading from those defending Chicago’s honor.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions Week 11 snap counts: Derrick Moore levels up; return of 3-safety sets
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 22: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers runs with the ball against Derrick Moore #8 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter at Ford Field on November 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions (8-2) beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 11, extending their win streak to six games and remaining atop the NFC North. This is the second time in the last four weeks that the No. 1 Defense in DVOA entered Ford Field and failed to slow a Lions offense firing on all cylinders. While the game ended 31-21, it wasn’t as close as the final score suggests, as the Lions defense continued to play complementary football and was willing to give up late-game points to drain the clock and secure a victory.

Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward.

Quarterback

Jared Goff: 58 (100%)

Josh Dobbs: 0 (0%)

Another top defense and another stellar day from Goff. He completed 20 of 28 for 279 yards and two touchdowns, navigated the pocket at an MVP level, gained 12 yards on the ground, including converting three first downs, and even got the Lions into victory formation.

“He should be in the MVP conversation, ” Lions center Juice Scruggs said of Goff post-game. “He’s been playing light-out all year, and I don’t think he gets enough respect in this league. He’s very underrated, and I think people are just starting to see how good he is.”

Running back

Jahmyr Gibbs: 43 (74%)

Sione Vaki: 13 (22%) — 12 special teams snaps (48%)

Jacob Saylors: 2 (3%) — 14 (56%)

Gibbs has hovered around the 75% snap range for a while, but his touches are the number to watch. He had 27 in this game, which isn’t far from his “plan” for the season, but they’ll likely need to keep trying to find ways to take pressure off him as we head into the final seven games of the regular season.

Vaki continues to roll as RB2, while Saylors found the field in victory formation.

Wide receiver

Amon-Ra St. Brown: 46 (79%) — 1 (4%)

Jameson Williams: 45 (78%)

Isaac TeSlaa: 23 (40%) — 1 (4%)

Tay Martin: 2 (3%) — 15 (60%)

DeAndre Carter: 0 (0%) — 8 (32%)

For the first time since the early parts of the season, St. Brown saw more snaps than Williams. It’s not a major change, but when everything else played out close to what we have seen over the last two months, it’s the only notable shift.

Tight end

Sam LaPorta: 53 (91%) — 1 (4%)

Brock Wright: 43 (74%) — 9 (36%)

Tyler Conklin: 17 (29%)

Collectively, this group all saw their snaps level up, as it was clear the Lions wanted the tight ends involved in this game, and they produced 122 yards on six receptions in this game.

“Yeah, it’s pretty good. Yeah, (Tyler Conklin) Conk’s added that little layer for us this year where he is a third tight end, but he can run routes, he can get out of the backfield and do some things, and it was good to get him that one, off schedule,” Goff said of having three tight ends at his disposal. “And then Brock (Wright) and Sam (LaPorta) have just been so reliable. The seams were open today, and we hit them on a few of those. Thought Sam played so well, and he’s been deserving of getting more touches like that, and it was good to see him get the ball a little bit.”

Offensive line

LT Penei Sewell: 57 (98%)

LG Christian Mahogany: 58 (100%) — 6 (24%)

C Juice Scruggs: 58 (100%) — 6 (24%)

RG Tate Ratledge: 57 (98%) — 6 (24%)

RT Blake Miller: 58 (100%) — 6 (24%)

LT/6th OL: Larry Borom: 1 (2%) — 6 (24%)

LG Miles Frazier: 1 (2%) — 6 (24%)

C Seth McLaughlin: DNP

The Lions offensive line is in rhythm, and against the NFL’s second-highest blitzing team, they allowed only eight pressures and one sack, according to PFF.

With the emergence of 13 personnel (three-tight-end sets), the Lions have almost entirely moved away from “Jumbo” (six-offensive-lineman formations).

Interior defensive line

3T Alim McNeill: 54 (78%) — 4 (16%)

DT Tyleik Williams: 30 (43%) — 3 (12%)

3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 28 (41%) — 3 (12%) — 3 offensive snaps (5%)

DL Levi Onwuzurike: 20 (29%)

3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP (Inactive)

With the Bucs rushing attack being their greatest offensive asset, we saw a bit more Tyleik Williams in this game opposite McNeill. Gill-Howard continues to see goal-line snaps on offense as an extra blocker, but it looked like he may have injured his leg on his final blocking attempt and needed to turn down post-game interview requests from Pride of Detroit to get treatment. On a short week, this will be worth keeping a close eye on.

EDGE

Rush End Derrick Moore: 55 (80%) — 4 (16%)

Rush End DJ Wonnum: 49 (71%) — 4 (16%)

Big End Tyler Lacy: 17 (25%) — 6 (24%)

Big End Ahmed Hassanein: 12 (17%)

Rush End Eric O’Neill: 6 (9%) — 12 (48%)

EDGE Tyrus Wheat: DNP (Inactive)

With Aidan Hutchinson on injured reserve, speculation ran high about how the Lions would replace his snaps, but in their first game without him, the answer was simpler than expected: increase Derrick Moore’s playing time.

Wonnum, Lacy, and O’Neill saw few changes to their snap counts, but Moore’s snaps increased significantly. Over the Lions’ first six games, Moore never saw more than 30% of defensive snaps, but that number climbed to 42% in Week 8, 58% in Week 9, 68% in Week 10—as a game replacement for Hutchinson—and 80% now that he’s a starter. He rewarded coaches with a half-sack, a team-leading seven pressures (per NextGen Stats), and a 19.4% pressure rate.

Fan favorite Hassanein finally got to play in his first NFL game, and while he was quiet in his 12 snaps, it’s a valuable first step for the developing defensive end.

Linebacker

MIKE/WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 55 (80%) — 13 (52%)

SAM/MIKE Derrick Barnes: 53 (77%) — 7 (28%)

WILL K.J. Britt: 25 (36%) — 9 (36%)

OLB/PR Trevor Nowaske: 22 (32%) — 18 (72%)

LB Joe Bachie: 0 (0%) — 15 (60%)

LB Owen Pappoe: 0 (0%) — 6 (24%)

LB Amen Ogbongbemiga: DNP (Inactive)

The Lions linebacker carousel continues to rotate weekly.  After losing Jack Campbell, the Lions leaned heavily on Barnes and Rodriguez in their first game without their leader. The following week, Barnes’ snaps stayed high, while Rodriguez stepped back and made way for Nowaske and Britt. This week, Rodriguez jumped Barnes in snaps for the first time this season, while Britt jumped Nowaske by a few reps.

While there has been little consistency beyond Barnes playing at least 75% of snaps, the rotation is working. Rodriguez secured a sack, Barnes was key in run defense, Britt made an important fourth-down stop early in the game, and Nowaske delivered a delicious sack to help close things out.

Cornerback

CB/NB Roger McCreary: 65 (94%) — 1 (4%)

CB Rock Ya-Sin: 63 (91%) — 1 (4%)

CB Khalil Dorsey: 8 (12%) — 13 (52%)

CB Nick Whiteside: 7 (10%) — 10 (40%)

CB Ennis Rakestraw: DNP (Inactive – Injury)

CB D.J. Reed: DNP (Inactive – Injury)

Safety

S Chuck Clark: 69 (100%) — 1 (4%)

S/NB Brian Branch: 68 (00%)

S Kerby Joseph: 46 (67%) — 1 (4%)

DB Andre Cisco: 5 (7%) — 6 (24%)

DB Christian Izien: 2 (3%) — 12 (48%)

DB Keith Abney: DNP (Inactive)

With Kerby Joseph’s return at safety, the Lions shifted their secondary usage, keeping McCreary and Ya-Sin almost exclusively on the outside and letting the safeties handle the middle of the field. In base sets, the Lions leaned on Branch and Clark—now wearing the green communication dot and the “C” on his jersey—and in subpackage sets, Kerby took Branch’s deep role, while Branch shifted into the slot/box.

“I think it actually slowed it down for me even more, just calmed the situation down,” Clark said of the returns of Joseph and Branch. “Two guys that have been in this system. I know it was some things out there on the field that we just talking about and it just naturally flow. Alright, cool. It felt good. Like I said, I kind of said this the other day, looking at the tandem of them to do all them from the outside being on different teams like, OK, them boys, they hooping. And actually be in the mix with them, it felt good.”

Specialists

K Jake Bates: 12 (48%)

P Jack Fox: 8 (32%)

LS Hogan Hatten: 8 (32%)

Bates missed from 53 yards on the Lions’ opening drive but was clean the rest of the way, connecting from 56 in the second quarter and on all four extra-point attempts.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions grades: Offense looking unstoppable vs. Buccaneers
lions.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 22: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) looks for a receiver during a play during the second quarter of a regular season NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Detroit Lions on November 22, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

The Detroit Lions moved to 8-2 with an emphatic win over the underrated Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Let’s take a closer look at Detroit’s impressive performance with our Week 11 report card.

Quarterback: A+

Jared Goff was absolutely phenomenal against a stingy Buccaneers defense. Through the air, Goff delivered some big-time throws, including his 57-yard bomb to Jameson Williams with Vita Vea right in his face. Despite being pressured on 46.7% of his dropbacks (fifth-highest of the week), Goff produced +0.39 EPA/ pass, the fifth-best production of the week.

Goff was also surprisingly impactful with his feet. Whether he was avoiding a pair of sack attempts to find a Tyler Conklin for a big gain, scrambling for a third-and-9 conversion or moving the chains on a pair of third-and-1 sneaks, Goff’s mobility—yes, mobility—proved to be a huge factor during high-leverage plays.

Running backs: B+

You wouldn’t think Jahmyr Gibbs had a very effective day running the football by looking at the box score. His 98 yards on 23 carries is far below his average, and even feels like it’s artificially inflated by a late 26-yard run (22 carries for 72 yards is 3.3 YPC). But Gibbs constantly kept the Lions ahead of the sticks with solid 4-5 yard runs on first down and short-yardage conversion.

In the end, the Lions rushed for a 53.8% success rate (third best of Week 11) and +0.28 EPA/rush (highest of Week 11). This was against arguably the best run defense in football, by the way.

Gibbs, to his credit, produced 76 rushing yards after contact (sixth most of Week 11) and his individual +6.1 EPA per rush was the best of the week.

Wide receivers: B

Jameson Williams was excellent against the Bucs, taking full advantage of the early injury to Bucs cornerback Jacob Parrish and destroying his matchup with backup Benjamin Morrison. It was a quieter day from Amon-Ra St. Brown and Isaac TeSlaa, who combined for just five catches for 37 yards and a touchdown (all from St. Brown). You could argue both had a drop or two, so this unit gets dinged a little.

But I also think their lack of production had to do with Detroit’s game plan to attack the middle of the field with their…

Tight ends: A

The Lions clearly saw a mismatch in Tampa’s zone defense vs. their tight ends up the seams. Detroit’s tight ends combined for six catches and 122 yards—their best collective performance of the season.

“The seams were open today, and we hit them on a few of those,” Goff said after the game .“Thought Sam played so well, and he’s been deserving of getting more touches like that, and it was good to see him get the ball a little bit.”

On top of that, the tight ends all remain drastically important to the run game and pass protection, and I think the trio did a fine job in those duties as well.

Offensive line: B+

On the surface, it doesn’t seem like a great day for the offensive line. I already mentioned the high pressure rate, and while Detroit’s running game was efficient, it was far from explosive. The yards gained were tough ones.

Still, pass protection was good enough for Goff to average 3.06 seconds to throw (sixth longest of Week 11) and only incur a single sack on the day.

And two of the biggest weaknesses facing the Lions rushing attack—poor short-yardage conversion and too many negative plays—were not an issue in this one. The Lions were stuffed on just 6.9% of rushes (third lowest percentage) and they were 7-of-11 on third downs.

Defensive line: B

Early on, the Lions’ defensive line was absolutely nails against the run. Bucky Irving had just 12 yards on nine carries at halftime. But in the third quarter, it felt like the Buccaneers were starting to find some creases up the middle.

As far as pass rush, it was a mixed bag. Detroit produced a 34.9% pressure rate (12th), but turned that into four sacks (10.8% sack rate was sixth highest). For the third week in a row, Derrick Moore produced five pressures—and he had a half-sack to move to 4.5 on the season. But if we’re being honest, there was a clear Aidan Hutchinson void in creating consistent pressure.

Linebackers: B

K.J. Britt had an outstanding fourth-down stop, as he continues to get significant playing time and make the most out of it. Malcolm Rodriguez (0.5 sacks, pass defended) and Trevor Nowaske (1.0 sack, 2 TFLs) continue to do solid work and make plays in Jack Campbell’s absence. Meanwhile, it was more up and down for Derrick Barnes.

Coverage continues to be a bit of an issue with this unit, as Tampa’s running backs combined for seven catches and 75 yards, although tight end Cade Otton was held to just one catch for 8 yards.

Defensive backs: B

I think we need to take a moment and appreciate just how impressive it is that Brian Branch does not look like he’s lost a step a year removed from his Achilles injury. He just about locked down the nickel position all day. And Chuck Clark—save a potential MA at the end of the first half—continues to be a difference-maker, showing why he didn’t go straight to the bench upon Kerby Joseph’s return. Joseph wasn’t much of a factor in his 2026 debut, as it looked like there was some rust to shake off.

At corner, it wasn’t Rock Ya-Sin’s best day. While he was never torched in coverage, he couldn’t make plays against Ted Hurst (five catches, 56 yards, 2 TDs) when in-phase. On the other side, Roger McCreary wasn’t tested much, but only gave up three catches for 22 yards and tallied a pass breakup.

For what it’s worth, I’m not docking this unit for the last drive and the pair of pass interference penalties. It’s garbage time. I do not care.

Special teams: D

Dave Fipp is not going to be happy this week. There were far too many penalties on this unit.

Holding on Nick Whiteside changed starting field position from 32-yard line to 14-yard line

Illegal formation on Malcolm Rodriguez cost 5 yards of field position

Blindside block on Malcolm Rodriguez change starting field position from 30-yard line to 13-yard line

That’s a total of 40 yards of field position impacted by special teams.

Tack on a missed 53-yard field goal from Jake Bates, four kickoff touchbacks from Bates, and one from Jack Fox on a punt, and it just wasn’t a great day. Kudos to Bates for making up for his missed kick with a 56-yard bomb, but I have much higher standards for this unit.

Coaching: B+

First off, we need to give the coaching staff a ton of credit for navigating the international travel for the last two games. The Lions had to deal with jetlag while the Buccaneers were coming in well-rested off a bye week, and Detroit matched—if not, exceeded—Tampa’s intensity and physicalness.

Additionally, the gameplans were solid on both sides of the ball. On offense, Detroit leaned on the passing game to open up the run game, and it worked to near perfection. On defense, they keyed in on taking away the run early, and they nearly pitched a first half shutout because of it.

However, I can’t give them an A, because I thought there were two key moments in this game that allowed the Bucs to hang around more than they should’ve. First, the defensive call in the final seconds of the first half was inexcusable. The only play for the Bucs there was to take a shot in the end zone, so there is no world in which Baker Mayfield should be able to find a one-on-one matchup for the score there.

The other came on Detroit’s first second-half possession, when Detroit was facing a third-and-inches. The Lions did such a great job the rest of the game taking what Tampa was giving them on defense, and they got too fancy here with a play-action pass that the Bucs sniffed out. A QB sneak, which has been extremely effective for Detroit over the past month, would’ve kept the drive alive. Instead, the Lions punted the ball away giving the Bucs a chance to take the lead.

Those may seem like minor quibbles, but they had drastic results and if, say, that Irving 80-yard touchdown didn’t get nullified, I think we may be looking at these two decisions as much more costly.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Bears odds: Detroit home underdogs on Thanksgiving
lions.body:
Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch (32) sacks Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

As the Detroit Lions enter Thanksgiving week, they’ve won six straight games, are 8-2 overall, and are 2-0 in the division, sitting in first place in the NFC North. This Thursday, they’ll host the Chicago Bears, who also enter this game at 8-2, but are 0-2 in the division, putting them in second place.

Despite the Lions’ better record and the game being at Ford Field in downtown Detroit, the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions +2.5 points.

In Ben Johnson’s first year as head coach, the Bears went 11-6 and won the NFC North. They beat the Packers in the Wild Card but lost to the Rams in the Divisional round, ending a season that exceeded expectations.

This offseason, the Bears made a few tweaks to their offense while overhauling half of their defense. On offense, priority No. 1 was replacing their center, Drew Dalman, who surprisingly retired. So the Bears traded with the Patriots for Garrett Bradbury, then drafted Iowa’s Logan Jones in the second round. At receiver, they traded away DJ Moore and replaced him with former Lion Kalif Raymond, who has stepped into a starting role in the slot and flashed.

On defense, the Bears lost all four of their top safeties (Kevin Byard, Jaquan Brisker, Jonathan Owens, and Chauncey Gardner-Johnson), their top linebacker in Tremaine Edmunds, starting NT Andrew Billings, and EDGE Dominique Robinson. At safety, the Bears made two splash moves: drafting Dillon Thieneman in the first round and signing Coby Bryant in free agency, who unfortunately suffered a season-ending injury, but they also signed Cam Lewis, who has since stepped into a starting role. Former Michigan Wolverine Devin Bush was signed in free agency to fill an Edmunds-sized void at linebacker, and Neville Gallimore was brought in to start at nose tackle. When Gallimore struggled, Chicago made a significant in-season trade, sending two first-round picks to acquire NT Jeffery Simmons.

The Bears opened the season by dropping 59 points on the Panthers and had Johnson talking about setting the NFL scoring record. The next week, the Bears scored only three points in a 9-3 loss to the Vikings. Wins over the Eagles and Jets helped them regain rhythm, but they fell to the Packers in Week 5—their third consecutive loss to an NFC North rival dating back to last season when they lost to the Lions in Week 18.

Since their 3-2 start to the season, the Bears have been on a roll, winning their last five games, rolling up over 30 points on the Falcons (31-23), Patriots (30-24), and Seahawks (34-17), but they have shown some kinks in the armor of late. Quarterback Caleb Williams was lucky to overcome a four-interception performance in Week 9 to beat the Bucs 27-24, and this past Sunday, he underwhelmed again, but Chicago’s defense delivered, and the Bears beat the Saints 21-13.

The Lions will host the Bears this Thursday in their traditional 1 p.m. ET slot on Thanksgiving Day at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan.

lions.headline: Discussion: What’s more impressive: Detroit Lions’ pass game or run game?
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 22: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions runs with the ball as Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions cheers in the background against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the fourth quarter at Ford Field on November 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions have won six games in a row and things are looking good ahead of a pivotal Thanksgiving Day showdown with the Chicago Bears.

The defense has impressed for more than a month, stringing together stalwart performances despite losing many of their key contributors. The offense, meanwhile, has looked sharp of late, dropping 35 points on the New England Patriots and 31 points on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Things have been so good for the Lions that two of their players are getting genuine Most Valuable Player consideration. Jared Goff has helmed one of the league’s best passing attacks, and aside from his two interceptions against the Patriots, has been playing near-flawless football. Jahmyr Gibbs, meanwhile, is putting up an extraordinary campaign out of the backfield, already breaking 1,000 rushing yards while also scoring an absurd 15 touchdowns across 10 games.

The Lions offense is firing on all cylinders, but which aspect of the offense has impressed you the most so far?

Today’s Question of the Day is:

Have you been more impressed with the Detroit Lions pass game or run game?

My answer: The run game. By all accounts, this was an impressive game for the Lions from top to bottom. That being said, I was really encouraged by how the run game persisted and eventually broke free.

Early on, it was tough sledding for the rushing attack. At the half, Gibbs had seven carries for 20 yards, an average of just 2.9 yards per attempt, far below the Lions’ standard. It was shaping up to be a hard-fought grudge match.

Some offensive play callers would shy away from their stalled rushing attack in the second half and opt to air it out instead. Drew Petzing had no qualms about letting Jared Goff uncork it, but it never came at the expense of the rushing attack. What has impressed me the most about Petzing is his adaptability and foresight. The Lions have such a good offense because they can take what isn’t working and spin it to their advantage.

Vita Vea is dominating the interior of the offensive line and stonewalling any rushing attack? In the second half, they started to Gibbs moving horizontally and outside the tackle box more. The Buccaneers boast a good run defense, but by playing away from that strength, the Lions started turning gains of two or three into gains of four or five. Over the course of a game, that makes a difference.

A running back like Gibbs is a ticking time bomb for defenses: it is not a question of if he’ll go off, but when and for how much. A lot of his yards on Sunday were tough yards—he rarely had a convoy blocking ahead of him. Instead, he is a master of earning those extra few yards on every down, whether it is with a quick juke or a well-time burst. Because of his explosiveness, he has the ability to turn almost any touch into a home run play. Not every play will be a home run, but opposing defenses cannot afford a single slip up against him. That is a high-wire act that few teams can manage.

The NFL is still a passing-focused league, but the Lions are showing how important a rushing attack can be. I genuinely believe that the Lions can run on any team in the NFL. Between Gibbs toting the rock, Petzing calling the shots, and the offensive line, receivers, and tight ends paving the way downfield, it’s not hard to see why this rushing attack is difficult to stop. I think the notion of “running to set up the pass” is archaic because it makes the run game sound like a tacked-on part of a good offense. The Lions are running the ball not because they want to open things up for their passing attack—they are running the ball because they are pretty dang good at it.

michigan.headline: Recruiting Roundup: 4-star QB ‘still going to Michigan’ despite OC change
michigan.body:
Welcome to the Recruiting Roundup, our twice-per-week series breaking down the latest developments on the recruiting trail for the Michigan Wolverines. We’ll keep you up to date on the top targets, the visits they take, the predictions that analysts make, and everything in between. Here’s what you need to know today…

Four-star QB still locked in with Michigan despite Beck’s firing

The quarterback that the Michigan Wolverines have verbally committed to the 2027 recruiting class is four-star Kamden Lopati. He is the No. 136 player in his class and he attends West High School in West Valley City, Utah. He originally committed under the impression that Jason Beck would be his offensive coordinator, but that is obviously no longer the case.

“I mean, it sucks,” Lopati told On3’s Ethan McDowell ($). “I love coach Beck and the staff that he came with. Still going to Michigan and locked in with them.”

The good news for the Wolverines is it doesn’t seem like that change is impacting Lopati’s recruitment.

“We didn’t expect all that to happen up there,” he said. “It’s definitely not the season any of them wanted, but it didn’t impact me in any way.

“I’m just always with Michigan and looking forward to getting up there in January and just starting off and being a Wolverine.”

Four-star DL targeting Victors Weekend for Michigan official visit

It’s really early on to begin talking about official visit season next summer, but Michigan is slated to host 2028 four-star defensive lineman Caleb Tucker for an official visit during Victors Weekend.

“I’ll definitely take an OV up there,” Tucker told On3’s McDowell ($). “I’m supposed to be coming back down for Victors Weekend.”

Tucker also has one of the best nicknames you’ll ever hear in football, as he goes by “Bonecrusher.” He was most recently in Ann Arbor for the Indiana game last month. Michigan narrowly lost in overtime, but Tucker still enjoyed the visit.

“The trip to Michigan was awesome,” Tucker said.

Michigan defensive tackles coach Larry Black is putting in all of his effort in this recruitment, as he also went and visited Tucker earlier this season. The two of them are forming a good relationship.

“Coach Black? That’s the guy right there,” Tucker said. “He’s a great guy. I like the way he coaches. I like the way he schemes everyone up.”

The Chicago native is the No. 142 player in his class.

Four-star 2028 RB ‘very high’ on Michigan

Another top target for the Wolverines in the 2028 class is four-star running back Cartae Ligon. He is the No. 155 player in his class and is from Chillicothe, Ohio. His interest in Michigan is “very high” despite the results on the field this year.

“No, it hasn’t changed at all,” Ligon told On3’s McDowell ($) when asked about his interest in the program. “I’m still very high on Michigan.”

Michigan running backs coach Tony Alford is one of the best recruiters in the entire country, as he has brought some great talent to Ann Arbor. He is ensuring Ligon that he knows he is a priority.

“It’s been amazing, calling every day and just texting me every day, saying what’s up,” Ligon said.

Michigan recently earned a commitment from one of Ligon’s teammates, 2027 three-star 2027 offensive lineman Conner Rutherford.

“I feel like they didn’t really look at him before he committed and stuff, and I think he deserved another chance, especially when he decommitted (from NC State),” Ligon said. “I knew he could play at that high of a level, and they liked what they saw and offered him.”

Ligon isn’t in a rush to make a decision, as he told McDowell that he will make his commitment “later down the road.” Still, Michigan sits in a very good spot with him as of now.

michigan.headline: Michigan Football Film Room: Wolverines build momentum before Ohio State showdown
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 21: Jalen Hoffman #42 and Travis Johnson #13 of the Michigan Wolverines celebrate after Hoffman's two-point conversion catch in the third overtime to win the game against the UCLA Bruins at Michigan Stadium on November 21, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The Michigan Wolverines defeated the UCLA Bruins 18-16. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

As of writing this, it’s November 22. For the generation below me, it’s another Sunday fighting off the hang-ziety and Sunday Scaries as the dawn of Monday looms. My generation is either herding kids or being herded by friends or partners for Sunday Funday. And for the generation above, it’s the day Kennedy was assassinated 63 years ago.

The most popular movie chronicling those events, JFK, is perhaps the most absurd, incredible, ridiculous, stylish, poetic, bong hit of a movie ever put to screen. A shameless portrait equal parts historical fiction and documentary, Oliver Stone’s personal exploration of the events of the 60s is a masterpiece for both the right and wrong reasons. After a three-hour roller coaster, the credits hit the screen, and the movie concludes with a quote from Shakespeare:

“The past is prologue.”

The past for Michigan entering last Saturday was a true tragedy. A team that had been left for dead by fans, the media, and the university itself. In fact, the expedited hiring of a new Athletic Director was for the not-so-secret reason of promptly firing Kyle Whittingham at the nearest opportunity. But this team and program showed something on Saturday that no one expected: heart.

On Senior Day at the Big House, there was a defiance to ensure the senior class left Ann Arbor with one more win in Michigan Stadium. Even facing an undefeated and top-five-ranked UCLA without leading receivers J.J. Buchanan and Andrew Marsh, leading rusher Jordan Marshall, and three starters on the offensive line, this team played with passion and physicality that have been nonexistent this entire season. Was it pretty? 10 Busch Lights couldn’t have beer-goggled this performance into anything resembling attractive. But it was gritty and resilient – adjectives that haven’t described this program since early November last season.

Although it was Senior Day, a handful of true freshmen on the offensive side of the ball stepped up in a big way to make this win possible. Running back Savion Hiter became the first freshman Michigan running back since Mike Hart (2004) with back-to-back 100-yard rushing games. Pass catchers Travis Johnson, Salesi Moa, and Mason Bonner looked like the Rugrats version of Cornelius Johnson, Roman Wilson, and Colston Loveland. Right tackle Marky Walbridge is laying a foundation to be one of the best tackles in the Big Ten in two years. And kicker Jacob Baggett single-footedly saved the game and season for the Wolverines.

But of course, the seniors did have their say.

Defensively, Zeke Berry, Jyaire Hill, Enow Etta, Trey Pierce, and Rod Moore all played with their hair on fire. The defense forced three turnovers and came up with stop after stop – as it has all season – to give the offense one final chance to win it. And with that chance – as it hasn’t done all season – the offense finally delivered, with prodigal son Bryce Underwood connecting with former walk-on senior tight end Jalen Hoffman in the corner of the end zone for his first career touchdown.

How can you not be romantic about football?

Heading into the final week of the season, Michigan has real momentum for the first time since… Oklahoma? Ever? If Michigan is going to ride this wave into Columbus, it needs to continue to build on the offensive effort and the defensive execution we saw against UCLA.

12-Personnel Long Trap

The first play of the game, interim offensive coordinator Jim Harding dials up his version of long trap. Long trap has been a staple of unemployed coordinator Jason Beck’s offense for years, but he never tailored it to fit the Wolverines. He famously failed with three different versions against Western Michigan. But Harding, as inexperienced as he is in play layering and sequencing, has grasped in two weeks what suits this offense better than Beck did in nine – POWER RUNNING.

Michigan comes out with double tight ends attached to either side of the line, one running back, a pair of receivers, and a quarterback under center. It’s beautiful. At the snap, left guard Manuel Beigel – who was playing defensive tackle this time last year, making his second career start on the offensive line – is going to pull down the line faster than a wide receiver picking up his DoorDash order and kick out the unblocked end man on the line of scrimmage. Everyone else on the line of scrimmage is going to pin a man down and running back Savion Hiter is going to press downhill before cutting behind Beigel’s block.

But how does this run turn into only the fourth 20-yard run that UCLA has allowed all season? True freshman wide receiver Salesi Moa. Moa is aligned at the bottom of the screen and has the unenviable task of going in motion to dig out the safety in the box. But not only does Moa reach the safety (who outweighs him by nearly 30 pounds), but Moa turns him outside to create a crease for Hiter to cut and turn this run into an explosive play. Culture is revealed by the way receivers block. Also, golf clap for right tackle Marky Walbridge, who, despite losing his balance, gets back to his feet and uses his frame to effectively box out the middle linebacker.

Harding is giving the offense plays to believe in and despite a rag-tag offensive line, the team is responding. This concerted effort to run the ball downhill should help to foster a rediscovered identity of physicality. It should set up play action. And it should help the offense find some success moving the football against the Buckeyes. But it all starts with at least 40 physical, downhill runs.

Single MUG Cover 2 Double T/E Stunt

This is nasty work from Jay Hill. Facing a third-and-eight, UCLA goes with an empty backfield and Hill shows pressure pre-snap. He’s been coming after the quarterback all day, so he knows the Bruins are expecting it. He walks linebacker Chase Taylor over the A gap and has fellow linebacker Troy Bowles hover over the stand-up three-technique (Jonah Lea’ea).

At the snap, Taylor and Bowles are both going to drop into a traditional two-deep, four-under zone coverage, while the defensive line is going to run a double stunt to confuse the five blockers and two chip players. Both defensive tackles crash into the B gaps, while the edges wrap around to shoot the A gap. The goal here is to create either a miscommunication or a one-on-one situation for either Dom Nichols or John Henry Daley.

Daley draws the double team, so Nichols wins the runway on this one and shoots down the vacated middle of the offensive line at full speed like a wide receiver who really loves Uber Eats. The right guard is able to recover just enough to chip him off his direct line, but the right guard also abandons his tackle to deal with Enow Etta alone. The threat of Nichols forces the UCLA quarterback to bail on the pocket and fall right into the outstretched arms of Etta, who tossed the right tackle out of his way. From the quarterback’s perspective, this was a lose/lose situation.

All 11 Wolverines are flawless on this play. Every receiver is accounted for in blanket coverage and the pass rush’s timing is metronomic. UCLA’s offensive line and quarterback are confused pre-snap, utterly lost post-snap, and there is danger waiting in every potential passing window.

Cover 1 vs. Long Trap Read

The lede was JFK so we have to mix in one conspiracy. I cannot prove this, but UCLA head coach Bob Chesney was planning on going for two and the win in regulation. After the twelfth play of the drive, an eight-yard gain set up first-and-goal from the Michigan three-yard line. With a timeout in hand, UCLA tries to smash it in on first down. Keep an eye on these four players – safety Chris Bracy, linebackers Chase Taylor and Troy Bowles, and farside defensive end Benny Patterson.

UCLA is running long trap with the tight end. Utilizing the H-back instead of the pulling guard makes it look more like split zone, but the offensive line isn’t zoning down. But just like the trap play above, this play is designed to hit on the trap side. The Bruins add in a read element with the quarterback in an attempt to freeze the trap player even more. In this case, that’s Patterson. However, his IQ and physicality immediately disrupt the timing of this play.

Seeing he’s unblocked, Patterson chops his feet, forcing the give, but even if he misreads it, look at Bowles in perfect position to hunt down the quarterback. The quarterback, however, does make the right read, yet Patterson again dictates terms by blowing up the tight end and closing the C-gap. If the running back wants to bounce it outside, Bowles is still lurking until he officially declares.

Taylor sets a hard edge on the near side, leaving only one lane for the running back to pursue. And unfortunately for him, Bracy flies downhill faster than a wide receiver answering the door when Postmates arrives and makes contact before the running back can reach the line of scrimmage. Smith Snowden and Rod Moore collapse to finish the play and although the running back’s momentum carries him down to the one-yard line, if Patterson doesn’t close the C gap, Bowles doesn’t eliminate the cutback, Taylor doesn’t set the edge, and Bracy doesn’t make contact as early as he does, this is a touchdown.

If UCLA scores a touchdown here on a power run, Chesney is 100 percent dialing up the wildcat jump pass for the two-point conversion and the win. If he connects on the slot fade against Snowden on the next play, it’s likely 50/50 if he goes for two. But if this converts, I know Chesney wanted to go for the win.

On Kyle Whittingham…

This will be the first time both Michigan and Ohio State have entered the matchup with each team having at least four losses since 1966. A game in which Michigan won on the road, 17-3, for what it’s worth. And this time, both head coaches could be coaching for their jobs.

Win or lose, Michigan has to make a decision on Kyle Whittingham immediately after the Ohio State game. The university cannot wait until after the bowl game due to the timeline of National Signing Day, the transfer portal, and the other coaching vacancies on the market. A decision has to be made as close to the final whistle as possible. And here lies the rub… With an improbable win over UCLA, what happens if Whittingham now wins in Columbus? When recent Michigan teams have faced a bowl-eligibility crisis in Week 11, the results have presaged the outcome in The Game:

2009 (Entered with five losses) – 21-point loss at Wisconsin; loss to OSU

2014 (Entered with five losses) – Seven-point home loss to Maryland; loss to OSU

2024 (Entered with five losses) – 44-point home win over Northwestern; win over OSU

Furthermore, no Michigan head coach has been fired after beating Ohio State. Technically, Bo is the only Michigan coach since 1947 to have beaten the Buckeyes in their final season, even if they retired or left of their own volition; lest we forget, Harbaugh was suspended for the game in 2023.

Zooming out, sure, Whittingham is a terrible interview and desperately needs to fix miscalculations on his staff, but if Michigan wins on Saturday, he will have as many ranked wins in 12 games as Sherrone Moore did in 26 and will also match Harbaugh’s first-season ranked-win total, with a chance to surpass that number in a bowl game. And, most importantly, it will prove the locker room still believes in his message when no one could have blamed them for tuning out the old man after the lows of this season.

Of course, in the era of unprecedented moves occurring daily, Whittingham could still be fired with a win. But you risk fracturing the locker room again and what if your top coaching candidates — similar to last season — turn down the opportunity or go elsewhere? Is firing Whittingham after 7-5 and a win over Ohio State worth it for Eli Drinkwitz?

But if Michigan loses to Ohio State, Saturday’s win over the Bruins could be chalked up to a death rattle. One last gasp of air before the final nail is driven into Whittingham’s coffin. With losses in three trophy games and a .500 bowl-dependent record – Michigan’s worst full season in 12 years – the message of “patience” is going to be received as well as a collegiate celibacy seminar. And then, the move on from Whittingham will be expected and welcomed — even for, sigh, an Eli Drinkwitz.

After 11 games, it comes down to The Game. One game to cap off one of the most absurd, incredible, ridiculous, and memorable college football seasons for all the right and wrong reasons. One game to decide the fate of two programs. One game to decide the fate of two coaches. Nothing before this matters; the past is prologue, and chapter one of the future will be written in Columbus.
