michigan.headline: Michigan Football hopes to ‘change narrative’ of 2026 season by beating Ohio State
michigan.body:
The Michigan Wolverines have endured a disappointing campaign under first-year head coach Kyle Whittingham, but finishing the season with a couple big wins could go a long way in changing the narrative of this year.

If you’re thinking you’ve heard this before, it’s because you likely have. Just two years ago, Michigan was sitting at 5-5 overall and in jeopardy of missing the postseason after a frustrating start to the season. However, the Wolverines finished the 2024 season with three straight wins to change the outlook of the season.

It felt like Michigan’s season was all but over and there was nothing to play for at the time. Looking back on the 2024 season, coaches, players and fans tend to remember it in a positive light, single-handedly due to an epic late-season turnaround. Michigan marched into Columbus and pulled off a stunning upset over the No. 2 Ohio State Buckeyes. The Wolverines then beat the No. 11 Alabama Crimson Tide in the ReliaQuest Bowl to finish the season with a bang.

Fast forward two years, and the Wolverines are in a similar predicament. Whittingham is hoping to replicate 2024’s late-season success, which all started with a win over the No. 4 UCLA Bruins last weekend. Now, they have their eyes set on emerging victorious in Columbus for the third straight time.

“A win could change the season a great deal,” Whittingham told the media on Monday. “We talked about that as a team last week. We still have a great opportunity to change the trajectory and narrative of the season, and put a much more positive light on it. We checked off the box in the first opportunity and now we have a second opportunity, so we’ll see what we can do with it.”

Michigan was sputtering after consecutive losses (MSU, Oregon) but found a way to bounce back and beat the Big Ten’s top-ranked team with an upset over UCLA at The Big House. There’s a ways to go to change the narrative of this season, but the result on Saturday certainly didn’t hurt.

“We looked at it as an opportunity to still have a positive end to the season and I’m so proud of how our guys played,” Whittingham said. “We played extremely hard and intelligently. If we can continue to carry that over into this week — the emotion, passion and intensity are there and present, but the thing that’s going to win this game is the preparation.”

Whittingham also spoke about how much a win over Ohio State could change how this season is viewed.

“It would certainly make it a whole heck of a lot better,” Whittingham said. “We could assist in starting to change the trajectory and narrative of this season, at least to a certain extent. We’re still not ever going to be thrilled with having five losses here so that’s not the case, but it would certainly go a long way into giving everybody a better feeling about this season.”

Michigan hasn’t come close to reaching expectations this year and Whittingham’s seat is as hot as it gets. But the Wolverines are still fighting to replicate 2024’s late-season turnaround, and an upset at Ohio State would be the next step.

michigan.headline: Game Ball
michigan.body:
Game Ball

Brian
November 23rd, 2026 at 3:09 PM

11/21/2026 – Michigan 18, UCLA 16 (3OT) – 6-5, 3-5 Big Ten
At one point deep into the game, the UCLA fan in front of me exclaimed "hey, that was a nice play" after Ty Dieffenbach sort of side-armed it to his tight end right before a Michigan defender blew him up. The Bruins gained eight yards and neared field goal range. They were ranked 4th in the country, trailing 10-3 to a team with less offense than a Ms. Rachel video. This guy in particular had presumably flown across the country to see his team finish the drill against an overmatched opponent. The reason his team was trailing was a Tommy Rees fumble that set Michigan up in the redzone.
In a similar situation I would not have been able to maintain this dude's level of good cheer.
As UCLA drove to tie the game at the end of regulation he and his son cheered without reservation at UCLA finally clambering down the field in fits and starts. I marveled at this dude's ability to care about the thing without being weighed down by it.
I have heard tell of West Coast football fans. From time to time I've been around them, having attended a couple Rose Bowls against USC. I found the USC fans to be—and let me state for the record that this is the pot calling the kettle black—annoyingly aloof and arrogant. By contrast, UCLA fans seemed like newborn baby deer, peering out wide eyed at a world of possibility they never knew existed. Most of them seemed to be having fun just being in a game at Michigan Stadium. It was the least Midwestern thing to ever happen in that stadium, the happy burblings of people saying "what a game" as UCLA tried to score the only earned touchdown on the night.
[After THE JUMP: Rod Friggin' Moore]

----------------------------------------
I marveled at UCLA fans' equanimity despite having much the same attitude. Saturday was an odd experience. I was pulled so lightly by the events going on in front of me. If Michigan did a good thing, it was good. If they did a bad thing, I expected it and defused it.
This freedom was underpinned by an assumption: Kyle Whittingham will not return as Michigan's head coach. Coupled with that is the inevitable fact that many of the players on the field before me were playing in their last game at Michigan Stadium despite the fact that almost no one of note is out of eligibility.
The stakes were suitably low and the results ephemeral, so I was free to root for Rod Moore and company without the weight of a season, a program, upon it. I just wanted these guys to go out with a win and go where they will.

Moore has had as many senior days as he's had non-senior days [Barron]
Moore, of course, told the Daily this week that if he had to go back and tell his freshman self something it would be to not stay:
“Leave after the national championship and go to the NFL,” Moore told The Michigan Daily bluntly. “I definitely would’ve left. I’ve been thinking about that a lot, but everything happens for a reason. … I don’t live with regret, but that is one thing that I will forever regret — is not leaving.”

The broadcast apparently spent some time contextualizing this, but I'd hope no Michigan fan needed any. Moore started as a freshman in the 2021 Ohio State game and is a co-equal legend with Sainristil and Mason Graham and Mike Barrett and everyone else on the 2023 defense. He could have had a veni, vidi, vici career, murdering his home state Buckeyes thrice and decamping for the League, but he stayed.
Amongst his peers on the 2023 team he was more or less alone amongst guys with an option. JJ McCarthy, Josiah Stewart, Kris Jenkins, and Junior Colson entered the draft with an option to return; Donovan Edwards, Max Bredeson, and TJ Guy either didn't have NFL profiles yet or were fullbacks. Other linchpins of the 2023 defense were sophomores with no option but to come back.
Moore and Moore alone stood at the pinnacle and said he wasn't done. I don't begrudge anyone their decision to leave, especially after the Last National Championship™. I do reserve a special place in my heart for the one guy who didn't have to stay but did.
And lo, how Rod Moore was repaid for that decision. A series of knee injuries cost him two consecutive years. Jim Harbaugh's replacement exited in year two because he slept with a direct report; his replacement historically cratered the offense while repeatedly throwing his own players under the bus in post-loss press conferences. Of course Rod Moore thinks he made a mistake by staying. So does everyone. It's a little painful to see him out there, an echo of what the program was just a few years ago, as the scoreboard details the NFL exploits of Blake Corum and McCarthy.
Moore got an opportunity to salvage a little something Saturday. Michigan sent him out alone to deal with the overtime coin toss. Michigan won it, then the defense held UCLA to field goals. One two point coin flip later:
‍↕️ https://t.co/6Mshk12GlP
— Michigan Football (@UMichFootball) November 22, 2026

That's a little something, there. I'm pretty checked out but no one's that checked out.
The thought of Michigan strolling to the locker room, burnished by an unlikely victory, warms the ol' cockles. I imagine Whittingham turned to Moore afterwards, detailed his illustrious career featuring three Big Ten championships, a national title, and calling game in the most important edition of The Game ever, and gave Moore a little piece of what he'd been missing ever since he passed on the boat to the NFL after 2023:

…
[slow, controlled blinking]
…
[attempt to be very UCLA about things]
…
Oh for fuck's sake!
On Senior Day! Rod Moore senior day! I can't with this guy and his thirty million dollar buyout that Warde Manuel gave him for no reason whatsoever.
From day one Whittingham has been contemptuous of the program here. He arrived asserting that "we will not become you," which hit different when it seemed like Sherrone Moore was a bigger chaos agent than Jason Beck. In press conference after press conference he's talked about how Michigan can improve through the portal or bitched about Dan Lanning's NIL; he categorically refused to fire Jason Beck and then fired Jason Beck a day later. He has been repeatedly baffled by the plays his own team calls. He walked off the field still wearing his unplugged headset after Michigan State.

he's a nihlist, dude [Barron]
Michigan could beat Ohio State by a trillion Saturday and I'd still want to ship this guy back to Utah. Michigan failed guys like Rod Moore and Bryce Underwood; Whittingham is a big part of that equation. I don't care why. He's 67; he's not getting better as a coach.
For everyone--Rod Moore, Kyle Whittingham, Warde Manuel, us—it's time to move on. For Moore, at least, let's hope its to better and brighter things than the last three years. For us, too, I guess. The others can go hang. Godspeed.

michigan.headline: Michigan Football readying for ‘generational’ Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith
michigan.body:
COLUMBUS, OH - NOVEMBER 14: Ohio State Buckeyes wide receiver Jeremiah Smith #4 seen in action during the game between the Ohio State Buckeyes and the Northwestern Wildcats at Ohio Stadium in Columbus, Ohio on November 14, 2026. (Photo by Jason Mowry/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

The 2026 college football season certainly hasn’t gone as expected for Ohio State. The Buckeyes enter The Game with a 7-4 record and barely hanging on to a spot in the AP Poll, with their College Football Playoff hopes completely out the window after losing at Nebraska over the weekend.

The season went off the rails the moment they lost starting quarterback Julian Sayin for the season when he suffered an elbow injury against Indiana. Across the board, the Buckeyes haven’t had the elite talent to make up for the loss, but they still have one player who’s capable of taking a game over — wide receiver Jeremiah Smith.

If you’ve been watching college football at all the past few years, you’re likely quite familiar with Smith. You could argue he’s been the best player in the nation the last three years, and even without his starting quarterback for half of the season, he’s still hurtling toward a Heisman Trophy and will be among the top selections in next year’s 2027 NFL Draft, if not the No. 1 overall pick.

Having only played three seasons, Smith has cemented himself as the most productive wide receiver Ohio State and the Big Ten have ever seen. He has set records for career receiving yardage and touchdowns in both school and conference history, while also securing the most career receptions in Ohio State history.

Smith benefits from his size (6-foot-4, 220 pounds) and speed, but also because Ohio State hasn’t had a second or third wideout emerge this season. For perspective, Smith’s 86 receptions this year are 12 more than the next seven wide receivers on Ohio State’s roster have combined.

So far, Smith has registered 1,482 yards and 17 touchdowns, and even with new quarterback Luke Fahey taking over as the starting quarterback, the game plan hasn’t changed for the Buckeyes — throw it to the big and fast guy wearing No. 4.

67-YARD JEREMIAH SMITH TOUCHDOWN!@OhioStateFB is on the board first@ATTBusiness pic.twitter.com/AzvQfIi50N
— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) November 21, 2026

Smith has found the end zone twice in his career against Michigan, but has been largely held in check by his standards with just a combined eight receptions and 75 yards in those two games. Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham, though, understands that Smith is still as good as it gets and demands a ton of attention.

“(Smith is) a generational receiver. A generational talent, I should say, at receiver. He’s the whole package,” Whittingham said on Monday. “He’s got the size, the speed, the strength, the hands, the route running ability, the toughness, the competitiveness.”

With Michigan’s defense coming off a dominant outing against UCLA — and Ohio State’s offense being much more limited in the second half of the year — one can imagine Smith will be a big part of the game plan for the Buckeyes. Additionally, Ohio State’s run game has been pretty unspectacular all year, and Michigan’s secondary has given up some big plays as of late while also being pretty susceptible to pass interference and holding calls.

In a game that’s sure to be low-scoring — the over/under is around 38.5 as of this writing — Ohio State’s best chance to score is directly through Smith, and he’ll probably need to double his combined output from the last two matchups against Michigan. For him personally, he’ll also need a big game to lock up the Heisman, with Utah quarterback Devon Dampier starting to close the gap.

While Ohio State as a whole is down this year and might not be as star-laden as we’re used to seeing, Smith will look to more than make up for the deficit against the Wolverines. If he doesn’t, it’ll likely be the start of a very long offseason in Columbus, as one of the Big Ten’s premier programs will have some serious retooling to do.

michigan.headline: This Week on State Street is Ready to Beat Ohio State
michigan.body:
This Week on State Street is Ready to Beat Ohio State

ByAZuniga
November 23rd, 2026 at 1:09 PM

On July 30, 2026, new Michigan football coach Kyle Whittingham commented at Big Ten Media Day about how “hate” might be too strong a word to describe the Ohio State rivalry.
“Hate is a strong word,” Whittingham said then. “… I just think that a rivalry can be intense and emotional without the hatred factor. I don’t think there's a place for that.”
This has made a lot of people very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move.
Four months later, we have arrived. Battered and weary, but we have arrived all the same. It’s the 122nd edition of the greatest rivalry in college football, but it’s one that has stripped away all the unnecessary frippery like Big Ten title and national championship implications. We’re down to the bare essentials on Saturday afternoon at The Horseshoe: One side wears Scarlet and Gray; the other side is in Maize and Blue. That alone is enough.
This is the last game of consequence for both programs this season.
“No coach is more important than the team.” This is not Kyle Whittingham versus Ohio State; it’s Michigan versus Ohio State. Let’s battle.
Here’s what to know from Kyle Whittingham’s press conference on Monday morning of Ohio State week:
Bryce Underwood is QB1 against the Buckeyes, though there have since been reports he’s dealing with a lower-body injury that “has his status in question.”
Jordan Marshall “hopefully will be back” against the Buckeyes, Brady Norton should be back, and Blake Frazier is “making progress.”
Michigan no longer has a “Beat Ohio” period in practice but Whittingham assures the rivalry has been taken seriously.
Hit the jump for a full transcript of Whittingham’s pre-Ohio State press conference, plus some commentary.

Here is everything Kyle Whittingham said at his pre-Ohio State press conference on Monday, Nov. 23. Commentary in italics:
Kyle Whittingham on the most impactful things he’s been told about the Ohio State rivalry:
I don't know if there's any one impactful thing. It's been so many impactful things. I mean, it's obviously one of the biggest rivalries in all of sport — not just football, but in all of sport. And it's obviously been well explained to me, and I knew a lot about it obviously before I got here. I mean, who doesn't? But I can't answer your question as far as the one statement, but we certainly understand, I certainly understand the magnitude of this game.
It's huge. There's no doubt about it.
Kyle Whittingham on if Michigan still holds a ‘Beat Ohio’ drill:
We don't call it the ‘Beat Ohio’ practice period, but we've definitely spent time on it, and meeting time, on-the-field time, obviously the signage in the building. It's present every single day of the year. And so that's something that has not changed and will continue to be emphasized.
AZ: The 'Beat Ohio' drill was a 9-on-7 inside-run drill implemented by Jim Harbaugh and Sherrone Moore. An air raid siren would mark the beginning of the period, and loud music would blare throughout.
As Trevor Keegan once described: "It's a physical period. It's really not as much about technique; it's about beating the man in front of you. I feel like that has been a culmination of where our toughness came from."
Kyle Whittingham on keys for Michigan against Ohio State this week and how different this week feels:
We'll get with our team this afternoon, with a team meeting, and talk about it.
And to me, excitement. The excitement of having the opportunity to be a part of this game, this rivalry. I've never been in the stadium down there. Never as a spectator, as a coach, as a player, never. So that's something that I'm looking forward to. And our players, obviously, the whole year, it's in the back of your mind every single day of the year. So it's something that I'm very excited about.
Kyle Whittingham on when Michigan learned of WR Andrew Marsh’s misdemeanor indecent exposure charge and why he felt a one-game suspension was appropriate:
Found out what was going on, geez, what day was it last week? Thursday of last week. First we had heard of it. And after gathering information and doing research, it was my decision. Didn't put that in the hands of the team. That was the decision I made to sit Andrew out last week.
AZ: Andrew Marsh is expected to return against the Buckeyes after serving a one-game suspension, as Whittingham said postgame on Saturday.
Kyle Whittingham on the spotlight on him this week and his relationship with Ryan Day:
Well, coaches are in the spotlight every week. I don't think that's any different. It's magnified this week, obviously. But I don't feel much different in that regard this week.
Ryan, we played Ohio State in the Rose Bowl, what, four, five, six years ago. Can't remember exactly when it was. And I had a chance to interact with him at that point. But I don't know him on a personal level. But just through competition.
AZ: That was a 48-45 Ohio State win in the 2022 Rose Bowl. Jaxon Smith-Njigba set a bowl game record with 347 receiving yards.
Kyle Whittingham on how Michigan has sought the right balance of downplaying versus emphasizing the rivalry:
I don't know if we downplayed it. I don't feel that we did that. But there comes a point where you can go over the top and you get diminishing returns from the players and the game itself. You gotta still stay within your framework and your process. But it certainly is emotion and passion that is there during rivalry week. It's gonna be intense and it's gonna be high. But like I said, if you get too far over the top, then it can give you negative results. So you gotta balance it as best you can.
Kyle Whittingham on what he did to emphasize the Ohio State rivalry this year:
We pay attention to it pretty much all year long. And spring ball, parts of it was devoted to that. Coaches, scout reports and prep this summer were devoted to that. The bye week, we took some time devoted to it. So yeah, it's been interspersed throughout pretty much the whole year.
AZ: Jay Hill last week said "one of the reasons why I came to the University of Michigan was to play in this rivalry."
Kyle Whittingham on what stands out about this year’s Ohio State team, and their quarterback in particular:
I spend most Sundays taking care of our game and corrections and evaluating what we just did. I did get started, obviously, yesterday on some of it. But the quarterback is the No. 2 guy, obviously, with the starter getting hurt several weeks ago. And so I’ll have a better answer for you that as the week goes on.
AZ: I found it a little strange that Kyle Whittingham couldn't or didn't give a more substantive answer about Ohio State, even at this point in the week.
Kyle Whittingham on what Urban Meyer told him about the rivalry and if their friendship is on pause this week:
Well, he certainly is a close friend of mine, like you said. And we've had conversations about it. When I first presented him with the possibility that I might be a candidate for this position, that was the first thing he talked about: ‘If you do get it, to be able to experience that game is going to be something special.’ And just elaborating on it. And that was really the first topic of conversation that we covered.
Kyle Whittingham on what it says about college football that Ohio State and Michigan are both having disappointing years:
I think the Portal has a lot to do with that. Teams are making big moves in one direction or the other each year. You never saw that, certainly not to this extent, before the advent of the Portal.
And that really has allowed teams to — essentially overnight at times — transform themselves and have a complete makeover. And also teams that can get gutted. I mean, there are certain teams that just go from being pretty good to not so good in a quick fashion.
And so the old 4-to-5 year plan to build a team, build a program, that's pretty much out the window. That doesn't apply anymore. And again, I attribute that to the Portal and the way that you can just completely make over a roster from year to year.
Kyle Whittingham on if he has a grasp on fan expectations about the Ohio State rivalry:
Yeah, I think so. I think I've got the flavor of it. And the intensity, like I said, and the passion. And just the widespread ripple effect of this game. I mean, it's huge. There's no way to say it other than it's a huge game. And we certainly understand that. I certainly understand that.
Kyle Whittingham on how a win over UCLA and Ohio State could change the tenor of the season:
Oh, it would change it a great deal. And we talked about that as a team last week — that, hey, we still have a great opportunity with the two games that we had left to change the trajectory of the season, the narrative, to an extent. Not completely, but to an extent, and put a much more positive light on it. And we checked the box in the first opportunity.
And now we've got the second opportunity. So we'll see what we do with it.
Kyle Whittingham on the excitement about the Ohio State rivalry:
Well, it doesn't surprise me at all. Like I said, the biggest rivalry in all of college football, without a doubt. I mean, it's not even close. And then, like I said, within the sports world, it ranks right up there. Just the passion and the history of it. I feel like I've got a great grasp of it.
I know our team has a great grasp of it. And as does our staff. So we're ready to play.
Kyle Whittingham on if he uses the 2024 Michigan team’s finish to the season as a blueprint:
I don't know if I looked at it as a blueprint, but an opportunity to still come out with a lot of positive things this season. And like I said, I'm so proud of the way our guys played on Saturday. They played extremely hard.
We played intelligently. We took care of the ball. One turnover. So many good things in that game, and we need to continue that and carry it over to this week. But it's still the emotion, the passion, the intensity, that is all obviously there and present. But the thing that's going to win this game is the preparation.
It still boils down to how you practice, how much film you watch, your visualization during the week. All those things that go in to prepare for a game is still the ultimate key. The other stuff adds to it, but the basis for it is the stuff you've got to do on a weekly basis.
… [Ohio State] is obviously the marquee game of the year, and you mentioned that some people would value that over a national championship. That's a pretty heavy statement because a national championship is a pretty special deal, and that gives you the flavor and the perspective on how a lot of people view this game.
Kyle Whittingham on what he’s seen from Bryce Underwood this season:
He's handled this as well as he could possibly handle it. The change in quarterback, being demoted to the No. 2 guy. Attitude never wavered. Work ethic never wavered. Preparation never wavered. He was just all-in every single day.
And I talked to him way back when the change happened. I said, ‘In this day and age of college football, odds are that you're going to get another chance this season.’ And sure enough, he got his chance on Saturday and did a good job running the offense.
We didn't put up huge numbers, but we took care of the ball. We ran the ball pretty decently. Obviously, the game-winner there at the end was well executed. Can't say enough good things about Bryce and how he's conducted himself and the teammate that he's been during this whole thing.
AZ: Bryce Underwood on how he views this season: "The way I took this season was more of a blessing. I took this as lessons being learned and how to move forward from it. The way you can show how to be a man is by facing adversity and how you take it on. That's been my main focus ... facing adversity and how I can recover from it."
Kyle Whittingham on Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith:
Incredible. Generational receiver. Generational talent, I should say, at receiver. He's the whole package. He's got the size, the speed, the strength, the hands, the route running ability, the toughness, the competitiveness. He's a terrific player. Terrific player.
Kyle Whittingham on if Jeremiah Smith should win the Heisman Trophy:
I haven't seen everybody and don't really even know all the candidates this year. Certainly, I would think he would have to be the frontrunner, in my opinion, based on what I know. Again, I haven't studied that out and figured out who the top three or four guys are.
AZ: Yeah, it should probably be Jeremiah Smith.
Kyle Whittingham on the amount of new players on both sides of the rivalry:
There is, as you mentioned, a lot of turnover. I think we had 56 new guys on our roster this year and a bunch of new coaches. That kind of goes back to what we discussed earlier about teams changing so dramatically from year to year. I don't feel there's going to be anyone in this entire building that doesn't know completely about this football game. Even though many of them haven't experienced it, they know what it's all about.
Kyle Whittingham on the statuses of Blake Frazier, Jordan Marshall and other injured players:
Blake, we're still waiting. He's making progress, I can tell you that, but we still do not have a definitive thumbs up or thumbs down for this week.
Brady Norton we hope to get back this week. He would have been available last week on Saturday in an emergency situation. JJ [Buchanan], out for the year, like we said.
Jordan Marshall: He hopefully will be back. It's going to be close, but we're hoping that we get him back this week.
AZ: Jordan Marshall spoke at length over the summer about wanting to get to the Ohio State game healthy after (essentially) missing last season's contest. Among other things, it makes me sad for him that he isn't getting that opportunity this year.
Kyle Whittingham on center Jake Guarnera playing through injury:
Jake Guarnera is a tough kid. He has played through a lot of pain. Again, we're not going to put a guy out there — our trainers, our medical staff isn't going to put anybody out there that is going to be in danger of furthering an injury. He has been able to endure a lot of discomfort and a lot of guys would not have been able to play with the discomfort that he's been able to play with.
Credit to Jake. He's a warrior.
Kyle Whittingham on if he feels this Ohio State game could make or break his tenure at Michigan:
No, I don't think this game is make or break, ultimately, in the big picture. It's certainly of huge importance and, like I said, it could assist in changing the trajectory and the narrative of this season to a certain extent. We're still not going to be thrilled with five losses ever. That's not the case.
But it certainly goes a long way into giving everybody a better feeling about this season, and what better way to finish things off than to beat a No. 4 team in the country and then your rival? It's a great opportunity for our guys.
Kyle Whittingham on if Bryce Underwood is QB1 against the Buckeyes:
Bryce is the guy. Bryce is the guy and Tommy is No. 2, and barring any unforeseen getting dinged up in practice or something like that, that's how it'll be.
AZ: The report from CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz, approximately 30 minutes later: "Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood is dealing with a lower body injury coming out of the Wolverines’ win over UCLA that has his status in question heading into the team’s game against Ohio State this weekend, sources tell CBS Sports."
Kyle Whittingham on the negative consequences of being too emotional about a rivalry game:
The negative consequences could be guys trying to do too much, playing hero ball, not just doing your job and focusing on what you need to do. Maybe some ignorant penalties creep in because you're so geeked up and you don't want that to happen. Once the foot hits the ball and it's in the air, you’ve got to go into game mode.
And again, the key will be the preparation throughout the week. The intensity and the emotion adds to the game, but the film study that you've done, what you've done on the practice field, all that far outweighs anything else. … You'd have to be living in a cave not to know the importance of this game — but there is a balance that you have to strike.

michigan.headline: Michigan no longer having a ‘Beat Ohio’ practice period shows Kyle Whittingham’s out of touch
michigan.body:
EUGENE, OREGON - NOVEMBER 14: Head Coach Kyle Whittingham of the Michigan Wolverines runs off the field at halftime during the game against the Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Ali Gradischer/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Michigan was coming off a 2-4 2020 season, the worst of the Jim Harbaugh era. Changes needed to be made, and Harbaugh made many. “Do it or die trying” was Harbaugh’s mantra about beating Ohio State and all of Michigan’s opponents. Another huge change Harbaugh made was changing the 9-on-7 practice period.

“It means everything to us; we got the music going, we got the energy going,” former Michigan linebacker Josh Ross said in 2021. “It’s exciting; we do it every single week.”

“We’re blasting music, smelling salts, everything. It’s a pretty physical period,” former Michigan offensive lineman Trevor Keegan said in 2021. “We love it!”

After Harbaugh introduced the ‘Beat Ohio’ practice period, Michigan went on to win three consecutive Big Ten Championships, culminating in a national championship win in January of 2024.

Despite the successes Michigan had with a portion of practice called ‘Beat Ohio’, Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham and his staff decided to do away with that name.

“We don’t call it the ‘Beat Ohio’ practice period, but we’ve definitely spent time on it,” Whittingham told the media on Monday. “Meeting time, on the field time. Obviously, the signage in the building. It’s present every single day of the year. That’s something that does not change and will continue to be emphasized.”

Kyle Whittingham says there is no more "Beat Ohio" practice period, but Michigan has devoted time all year to preparing for the Buckeyes pic.twitter.com/dxGeYOStrt
— Clayton Sayfie (@CSayf23) November 23, 2026

Whittingham said people would have to be living in a cave to not understand the importance of the Michigan-Ohio State rivalry, yet he made a change that strips the importance of the rivalry a bit. Whittingham called it the biggest rivalry in all of sports, yet got rid of the ‘Beat Ohio’ period of practice, which is known to be the most physical and tenacious. It seems like a counterintuitive decision.

Whittingham already lost to another huge rival, Michigan State, and his comments leading up to that matchup weren’t inspiring either. Whittingham gave MSU bulletin board material, calling it the “Super Bowl, particularly for them” while referring to Michigan State as Michigan’s “second-biggest rival.” The 16-6 loss to Michigan State meant Michigan had to surrender the Paul Bunyan Trophy to Michigan State, which was just one of two rivalry trophies they lost this season.

Michigan also surrendered the Little Brown Jug to Minnesota after losing to the Golden Gophers in Minneapolis for the first time since 1977. Heading into the game, Whittingham said “every game’s a trophy game” to him and didn’t want to “put any more emphasis” on it.

Things are adding up that Whittingham doesn’t understand the magnitude of Michigan’s rivalries — opponents always give Michigan their best — that’s what happens when you’re the winningest program in college football history. If Michigan beats Ohio State on Saturday, removing the ‘Beat Ohio’ drill will be a meaningless talking point, but if Michigan loses, it’ll be another example of changes Whittingham has made that seem like a clear mistake.

When Whittingham was hired last year, he said, “You will become us, we will not become you” — and that’s just not how things work — you will become Michigan, or you will not be here long. But in defense of Whittingham, he calls former Ohio State head coach Urban Meyer a “close friend” —perhaps that’s reason enough to think there are some things about the rivalry he doesn’t get and maybe never will.

michigan.headline: Report: Michigan QB Bryce Underwood dealing with injury heading into Ohio State game
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 21: Bryce Underwood #19 of the Michigan Wolverines runs the ball during the first half against Anthony Sacca #39 of the UCLA Bruins at Michigan Stadium on November 21, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

At his press conference on Monday morning, Michigan head football coach Kyle Whittingham said that sophomore Bryce Underwood is set to start in The Game this weekend against Ohio State.

However, we’ll see if he’s able to even play at all. Per 247Sports’ Matt Zenitz, Underwood is dealing with a lower-body injury that he suffered during Saturday’s stunning upset win over UCLA. His status is “in question” heading into The Game in Columbus this weekend.

Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood is dealing with a lower body injury coming out of the Wolverines’ win over UCLA that has his status in question heading into the team’s game against Ohio State this weekend, sources tell @CBSSports https://t.co/8hkCLxfbfB pic.twitter.com/2DH8FTR4j1
— Matt Zenitz (@mzenitz) November 23, 2026

Underwood has had quite the roller coaster season. He started the first six games of the season before freshman Tommy Carr took over after halftime of the Penn State game. Carr was then benched two weeks ago during the game at Oregon, and Underwood has taken every snap since.

Despite the injury, Whittingham told the media on Monday morning that Underwood is “the guy” at quarterback, and that “barring anything unforeseen, getting dinged up in practice or something like that,” he will start against the Buckeyes on Saturday.

Underwood completed just 11-of-24 passes for 127 yards and one touchdown on Saturday vs UCLA. He also ran 13 times for five yards, losing one fumble in the process. On the season, he has completed 85-of-156 passes (54.5 percent) for 1,077 yards, six touchdowns and six interceptions, while also running 76 times for 230 yards and an additional two scores.

Should Underwood not be able to play in this one, Carr will be the next man up for the Wolverines. The true freshman has completed 67-of-106 passes this season for 686 yards, two touchdowns and three interceptions. He’s also ran 49 times for 138 yards and three touchdowns.

Michigan vs Ohio State is set for a noon kickoff on FOX.

msu.headline: Women’s Soccer Advances, Men Kicked Out
msu.body:
The NCAA Soccer Tournaments began this weekend with both the Michigan State Men’s and Women’s Teams hosting games.

The Spartans Women earned a #1 seed and faced 16th-seed Central Connecticut State on Saturday.  The game went the way a 1-vs.-16 game should go.  MSU won 7-0 to advance to the round of 32.  The Spartans had two goals each from Bella Najera, Kennedy Bell, and LJ Pearcy along with one from Lacey Kindel.  After leading 4-0 at the half, MSU got both their 2nd and 3rd string goalkeepers in after halftime.  None of the 3 goalies had to record a single save.

Here is the first Spartan goal, which proved to be the game winner.

Bella Najera scores her FOURTH goal of the postseason!  Sargeant and Briggs with the assists to give MSU a 1-0 lead. pic.twitter.com/xOTMEYdkRD
— Michigan State Women's Soccer (@MSU_wsoccer) November 21, 2026

MSU will host their round of 32 game as well.  That game will be this coming Friday, November 27, against Xavier.

The MSU Men also earned the right to play their first game at DeMartin Stadium as a 4-seed.  Unlike the women’s tournament with 64 teams, the men’s tourney only has 48 teams, so the top 4 seeds in each region get a bye to the round of 32.  MSU hosted Marshall today after the Thundering Herd took down Bowling Green on Thursday.

After 90 scoreless minutes, the game went to overtime.  There were no goals in the extra sessions either, so the game headed to penalty kicks.  Even as the higher seeded team and the home team, Marshall outperformed Michigan State for large portions of the game, winning the shots-on-goal battle, 8-5.  The Spartan goalie, Jake Grekowicz, made a couple of challenging saves in the overtimes that nearly ended the game.

In penalty kicks, Marshall was the first team up.  Both teams made their first two attempts.  In the third round, Marshall converted but MSU’s shot was saved.  Each team made their 4th attempt, so Marshall led 4-3 heading to the 5th with a chance to win with another successful PK.  Sadly, Grekowicz was unable to make a save and Marshall picked up the win.

Had MSU won, they would have hosted the round of 16 game as the 1-seed in the region, Akron, was knocked off by Wake Forest earlier in the day.  The season comes to an end for the Men’s Team.

The Lady Spartans move on.  Their 7-0 win was the second largest victory in the tournament’s opening round; Alabama beat Jackson State, 12-0!  Get ready to tune in to that game on Friday to root on the Green & White as they look to advance to the 3rd round.

msu.headline: El Niño hits Spartans in The Weather Report
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 20: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks celebrates his teammates second half touchdown run against the Michigan State Spartans at Spartan Stadium on November 20, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Lots going on in the world of MSU sports this weekend. So, we thought let’s have some weather report fun and incorporate basketball, hockey and football all into this week’s report. Football was an ugly blood bath that we all saw coming. Hockey pulls off a split but had its own blood bath brawl in Yost. Basketball saw some solid bench action but the post is not looking good with the center position. Fellow TOC writer O helped out with this report and the basketball sun and cloud are coming from him. Without further adieu let us step into some sunshine.

Sun #1

My first sun is for the Spartan football team and coaches. They lost 45-7 you say, how could you possibly award the team a sun? This team has looked bad, and have had some very ugly games. This team has also had injuries that have superceded the last two years and those years were bad. What has changed this year is character. The team has character and fight. They are giving their best and not giving up. The number of underclassmen getting playing time, the number of athletes that are not the four stars Oregon is sending out there are all getting strong character development in Spartan grit. Fitz has the team playing. I’d be interested to see if he can get better athletes and take a good look at conditioning and what is going on with all these injuries. I know there is one more game but next year will really be the year to see what Fitz can actually potentially do.

Sun #2

Sun two brings us to the ice. MSU hockey has been off to a tough start and has been disappointing. Struggling to find their chemistry and identity with all the youth and lacking a true leader. Well, this weekend against the weasels MSU had an opportunity to perhaps turn the season in the right direction. Friday was an ugly game where the Spartans were manhandled and it all started with an early power play that had MSU behind practically from the start. Then we get to the melee. The hip check that the weasels felt very offended by. Barnhill and Vansaghi may have fought life back into this team. Even with both players suspended for game two and into the OSU series, they maybe let out frustrations of an entire team in an early season. Saturday night, an entirely different MSU team took the ice. Down defenders, Ward and Jurecki brought energy and the sticks were active Saturday. MSU out shot, out played, and out scored the number one team in the country. They looked like the team we have been waiting for. Yes, the weasels were short forwards, but MSU was down defenders. Ravensbergen looked outstanding, except when he left his post open, but still had the shut out. This might be a breath of fresh air that they needed to get into the winning column. The team is talented, now let’s continue to play like it.

Sun #3

Our basketball sun is going to Kur Teng. Teng had a career high 24 points on 8/11, and 5/8 from 3. Teng showed he can be a reliable shooter for this team. This allows the team to not rely on Scott and Jervis and sometimes Fears for all the perimeter shooting. Teng has always been smooth from three but has never been consistent or had a break out performance. Hopefully Teng can get hot and be a weapon that draws coverage which can perhaps open up some paint play if the MSU big men can handle it.

Cloud #1

Football cloud goes to the teams health. MSU was doubled in yardage, had two turnovers, were terrible on third down and I’m still giving the cloud to health. The injuries on this team need to be figured out. Injuries have haunted this team for a few years now. So, what’s going on? Is there something going on in conditioning or practices? Is it dietary? Is it really just bad luck? Conditioning coaches have changed and we still have the problem. This year though, was unbearable. The injuries were so much it had to be difficult to game plan when you don’t end up having the players you need on the field. It is nearly impossible to be competitive against an Oregon with third string players and a freshman QB.

Cloud #2

As much as the brawl helped inspire my hockey sun, that same brawl inspires my hockey cloud. Losing Barnhill and Vansaghi for one game is bad enough. The reprucussions of suspensions could be greater and have implications down the road. Having a significant penalty means the two are going to have to stay out of trouble or a worse suspension will come their way. That is a tough ask for a player like Vansaghi who is the agitator  for MSU. He is the guy that comes to the defense of his teammates and will throw a punch at anyone. To have him have to change his way of play could be a learning process. In a team that needs a bit more leadership, Vansaghi is a guy that can provide that, the chip on the shoulder, and the aggression. MSU needs him, so the suspensions will be something to keep an eye on.

Cloud #3

Our basketball cloud has been hinted at some but we can officially say it now goes to the centers. Taylor, McCulloch and Bonke had three combined field goals. They had six turnovers. None of them can be relied upon to be fed the ball in the low post and make a move to beat a defender. They are only scoring on rebounded put backs or a wide open Fears feed. To make things worse, the coaching staff didn’t even try to run any of those sort of plays. Bonke has been disappointing all season and Taylor is still developing. Regardless, the Spartans need a lot more production from the big guys in the paint. MSU typically struggles at the arc but has had some success there this season. If they can get stronger in the block and stay hot outside, they will be very difficult to beat. Hopefully, they can work out these kinks before the schedule gets even tougher in B1G play.

There we have it. As a big follower and fan of MSU hockey, I was very happy to see this team look like itself and take down number 1 at Munn. That was my favorite moment of the weekend. The lineup changes may be the key to staying hot on the ice. As always, I look forward to seeing where your clouds and suns lie in the comments. I wish you all a Happy Thanksgiving and be thankful there’s only Rutgers left on the football schedule. Go Green!

msu.headline: Instant Recap: Michigan State gets stomped by Oregon
msu.body:
Michigan State’s Derrick Simmons, left, tackles Oregon’s Da'Jaun Riggs during the first quarter on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 in East Lansing. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Whew, boy. That was the worst loss of the season.

It was all Oregon tonight. Michigan State’s offense struggled early, and Oregon scored halfway through the first quarter to give the Ducks a 7-0 lead behind a Brandon Smith 5-yard touchdown run.

Frederick Moore had a nice one-handed snag right before the second quarter started, but Liam Boyd would miss a 47-yard field goal for Michigan State’s first chance to put points on the board. The offense was starting to look solid behind Kayd Coffman’s play, but he would trip while running out of the pocket to turn the ball over on a 4th-and-3 from Oregon’s 28-yard line.

The defense did their best to keep the Spartans close, but their special teams did not. Chrishon McCray would muff the next punt by the Ducks to allow Oregon to take over in the redzone. The defense held tough and forced them to kick a field goal, and it made it a 10-0 game. Near the end of the first half, Dan Lanning called a fake field goal where the Ducks’ kicker was able to run it in from 15 yards out to give Oregon a 17-0 lead heading into halftime.

Once that fake field goal scored, it felt like the game was already out of reach.

Oregon opened up the second half with another touchdown run, this time from Simeon Price, to put them up 24-0.  Michigan State would respond with a touchdown of their own with a direct snap from the 1-yard line by Jaz Patterson, though it would be the only points they scored all night.

Both Brandon Smith and Simeon Price would add another touchdown run each for the Ducks, and Dylan Raiola found Dakorien Moore for a nice one-handed touchdown pass as Oregon continued to pile on the points. Oregon would go on to win 45 to 7. Michigan State moves to 3-8

Kayd Coffman completed 10 of his 19 passes for 106 yards and one interception. Jaz Patterson handled 16 carries, but only managed 26 yards. Brandon Tullis added 25 yards on eight carries. The Spartans’ leading receiver was Fredrick Moore with 31 yards on two catches.

It was a brutal loss, and one of those games where you wish it could’ve ended by the end of the third quarter, as Oregon kept putting more and more points on the scoreboard. Luckily for the Spartans, it’s not the end of the season, and they’ll finish it off with a matchup at Rutgers on Thanksgiving weekend. Let’s hope they can finish the season with a win.

Go Green!

tigers.headline: Tigers sign right-hander Luis Gil to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
Apr 26, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Luis Gil (81) delivers a pitch during the second inning against the Houston Astros at Daikin Park. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Tigers made another minor move on Sunday to shore up their pitching depth. Jeff Passan reports that the Tigers have signed RHP Luis Gil to a one-year deal worth $2.3 million, with a potential two million more in incentives. The deal is still pending a physical. Gil was non-tendered by the New York Yankees on Friday after a rough season on the mound for the 28-year-old veteran.

Gil’s career has already been a pretty wild ride despite his relative youth. The six-foot-three, 215 pound right-hander was initially signed as an international free agent out of the Dominican Republic as a teenager by the Minnesota Twins. In 2018, the Twins dealt him to the Yankees for outfielder Jake Cave. Gil developed into an excellent prospect in the Yankees’ system with eye-popping strikeout numbers, and eventually made his major league debut in 2021. The next season he blew out his elbow and required Tommy John surgery. He returned in 2024 and put together a strong campaign that earned him the AL Rookie of the Year award. A lat strain in 2025 and back issues in 2026 have limited him in the interim to just 84.1 innings over the last two seasons.

There are some reasons for optimism. Gil still has good velocity, sitting 95.3 mph on his fourseamer in 2026, though that’s down over a full mile per hour from his peak a few years back. He has good riding action on the pitch at the top of the zone, along with plus extension. His slider and changeup are both quality plus pitches. At his best he’s electric. He just hasn’t been able to stay on the mound long enough to get in a groove the past two years. His command has never been particularly good, and his walk rates have spiked as the injuries took their toll, but he’ll throw enough strikes to make it work if healthy.

We’ll be curious to hear what Tigers’ president of baseball operations, Scott Harris, has to say about this acquisition. There’s a very good argument that Gil would be better off as a reliever. He topped out at 98.4 mph in 2026, despite the ongoing back troubles. If he can sit 97-98 mph in short bursts he’d be pretty electric with a plus slider-changeup combination. At the same time, he can come to camp as starting depth if needed as well.

Hopefully the medicals come back clean. The Tigers have not had much success keeping their pitchers healthy at any level of the organization. That’s a leaguewide problem, but the Tigers have had it worse than many if we put the whole farm system into the equation. The club has already made changes this offseason, hiring Scott Peters as their new medical director and Jeremiah Randall as head athletic trainer and physical therapist, so there’s clearly an emphasis on trying to address the problem.

Ultimately, this is a small, low risk move of the sort Harris favors. Yet Gil has a lot of talent if his body will just cooperate and the club could come out way ahead with this signing if they can get him right.

Right-hander Luis Gil and the Detroit Tigers are in agreement on a one-year, $2.3 million contract, sources tell ESPN. Gil was nontendered by the Yankees this week and found a home in Detroit with a deal, pending physical, that includes up to $2 million in performance bonuses.
— Jeff Passan (@JeffPassan) November 22, 2026

tigers.headline: Assessing the Tigers payroll in the wake of Troy Melton’s extension
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers CEO and Chairman Chris Ilitch, manager A.J. Hinch and President of Baseball Operations Scott Harris and talk during Spring Training Tuesday, February 21, 2023. Tigers9 022123 Kd3999 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

While the deal isn’t fully official until the medicals are completed, the Detroit Tigers have come to terms with right-handed starting pitcher Troy Melton on a long-term extension offer. The deal reportedly guarantees Melton six years and $46.5 million, with incentives and a club option for the 2033 season that could take the contract to a total of $80 million over seven years.

This is a pretty smart decision from both the Tigers and the 25-year-old Melton. Our thoughts quickly turned to potential extensions for talented youngsters like Jackson Jobe and Max Clark. The club already has AL Rookie of the Year Kevin McGonigle, as well as infielder Colt Keith signed to long-term extensions. It will be interesting to see if the Tigers pursue extensions with their other talented young players prior to the December 1 lockout of the players by MLB owners. They don’t want to get stuck with too much guaranteed money on the books for the long haul, but at the same time these contracts are certainly very team friendly as long as the players involved produce as expected.

Our next thought was how this sets up the Tigers payroll for 2027. The Tigers entered the 2026 season with a payroll that was pushing towards the $244 million luxury tax threshold. However, after trading away three of their most expensive players in Tarik Skubal, Casey Mize, and Jake Rogers, all of whom were in their final year of arbitration eligibility prior to free agency, the final estimated Tigers payroll for 2026 came down to $195 million according to FanGraphs.

FanGraphs’ Roster Resource now estimates the Tigers’ 2027 Opening Day payroll at $169 million in the wake of Melton’s extension. That total would’ve put the Tigers 15th most in payroll in the major leagues in 2026, right in the middle. These are the salaries for their free agent deals and extensions on the books for 2027.

Framber Valdez – $47.5M

Javier Báez – $24M

Emilio Pagán – $11.5M

Kyle Finnegan – $10M

Drew Anderson – $8M

Troy Melton – $7.75M

Colt Keith – $4.77M

Kevin McGonigle – $2.75M

Jacob Waguespack – $1.3M

In addition, the Tigers do have a few arbitration eligible players estimated to make over $5 million in 2027. Riley Greene is estimated to earn $9.3 million, while Spencer Torkelson is estimated at $7.7 million for the 2027 season. Those two players are under team control for 2027-2028, and will then be free agents in 2029.

Zach McKinstry is estimated to make $5 million next season, while both Will Vest and Kerry Carpenter are estimated to make $4.4 million and $4.1 million, respectively.

So, looking forward to the rest of the offseason, the Tigers are still in fine shape to go make a big signing or just continue to build up their pitching staff and possibly hunt for a better bat in a part-time role. Ihey were willing to spend something like $240 million in 2026. That doesn’t mean they’re planning on keeping payroll that high year after year, but it seems likely they could add another $30-40 million in payroll this offseason and still be well short of their 2026 Opening Day payroll projection.

There’s room to spend. It’s more a question of a lack of major impact players that fit this offseason. Presumably there’s also some trepidation about signing any big free agent deals with so much up in the air this offseason. With the CBA negotiations and lockout coming, most teams would prefer certainty as to what the sports rules and payrolls are going to look like under the next CBA before making any huge commitments. Some teams will obviously make exceptions for Tarik Skubal and a handful of other top free agents, but the Tigers don’t seem like they’re going to be involved with those players.

Still it’s interesting to consider the Tigers payroll situation in light of the possibility that the owners do get their way and there’s a cap and floor instituted for 2028 as proposed. Under the owners’ most recent proposal, the floor would be $180.2 million against a hard cap of $258.2 million. Part of that would involve smaller market teams like the Tigers getting more in revenue sharing money, but actually being required to spend up to that $180.2 million level. Since the Tigers were willing to spend roughly $240 million for the 2026 season, with additional league revenue coming in they would likely be in a position to spend close to that level on a yearly basis going forward.

The Tigers have their second biggest annual salary coming off the books after 2027 as Javier Báez reaches free agency. That takes $24 million off the payroll heading into 2028. And, should Framber Valdez bounce back in year two in Detroit with a good season, there’s a fair chance he would choose to decline his 2028 player option with the Tigers, worth $35 million, and head back to free agency. A cap and floor system might have some impact on Valdez’s desire to return to free agency a year early as well. Even so, while the Tigers’ expenses will increase elsewhere as players get raises and then reach arbitration, there is plenty of money bound to come off the books in the next few seasons as well.

Obviously, this is speculative as there’s nothing to suggest the players are going to give the owners what they want in the CBA negotiations. Still, thinking through the general possibilities shows the Tigers in pretty good shape going forward whether a cap and floor system is put in place or not. They could clearly afford even a $400 million offer to Tarik Skubal if they thought that was the best way to allocate their payroll. With several talented younger players already locked up on long-term deals, minimal major commitments to older players, and with a still good farm system brewing up more major league talent to come, the Tigers future looks pretty bright if the front office can finally make the right moves to put them seriously into contention on a yearly basis.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign RHP Troy Melton to a six-year extension
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Troy Melton #52 of the Detroit Tigers delivers a pitch against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jayden Mack/Getty Images) | Getty Images

While we were waiting for non-tender deadline news, and there was none involving the Tigers, who tendered contracts to all eligible players other than Matt Vierling, who was already DFA’d on Tuesday, the club had other business instead. Multiple reports emerged on Friday evening that the Tigers have inked right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year contract extension that guarantees him $46.5 million with incentives and a club option for 2033 that could max out at $80 million over seven years. The deal is still pending a physical and not officially announced yet.

The hard-throwing right-hander will turn 26 years old in about two weeks. He has one year and 68 days of MLB service time currently, so this deal arrives as Melton was still five full seasons from free agency. Exchanging an extra year until he’ll reach free agency, and potentially two years if the Tigers use their club option, to guarantee himself at least $46.5 million is a pretty good deal for both sides. Melton wouldn’t have reached free agency until he was headed into his age 31 season, and with pitcher injuries being what they are, there’s always the risk that he wouldn’t be as valuable by that point in his career.

From the Tigers’ perspective, they locked up six years of Melton at less than eight million a season, a bargain for a pitcher who is on track to be worth roughly 2 WAR per season if he continues on his current track. Of course, the Tigers, and no doubt Melton himself, expect continued improvements in the years ahead. There are plenty of incentives that could make the deal much more lucrative for Melton, but if he earns them the Tigers won’t have any problem paying him extra. With a 96-97 mph fastball with big extension that can reach triple digits, along with a deep and developing arsenal of pitches including a sinker, cutter, slider, curveball, and splitter, the potential here is pretty enormous. Melton just hasn’t found the strikeout touch consistently to take him into the upper tiers of starting pitchers around the league quite yet.

2026 was Melton’s first full season as a major leaguer after debuting in the second half of 2025 in a mixed role that included starts and high leverage relief appearances, and some good performances in the postseason. This season didn’t get off to a good start as Melton had some elbow inflammation in spring camp. The Tigers shut him down and took their time, getting him back on the mound in late May.

Melton went on to make 20 starts totaling 114.1 innings pitched. He posted a 2.76 ERA and a 4.09 FIP over that span. He keeps balanced splits, leaning on that deep repertoire of pitches. With more consistency from his good slider-split combination, he should be able to strike out more hitters. For now, the fact that he attacks the zone aggressively and doesn’t issue many walks, while controlling contact, is a great foundation to build on going forward.

His season didn’t end well, as his performance fell off in late August and into September. Eventually he was shut down after a start on September 20 with forearm tightness and general arm fatigue. Reports have since emerged that he’d avoided any serious injury. The Tigers must be pretty convinced in his medicals to have extended the extension offer, and perhaps those issues during the season convinced Melton that it was a good idea to come to an agreement and guarantee himself the money now.

One also wonders what this says about the status of Jackson Jobe and Max Clark, two other highly talented youngsters who have shown some nice flashes in the major leagues but are really just getting started. It will be interesting to see if this is just the first in a flurry of extensions designed to provide stability and cost certainty with the Tigers top young players just as the sport heads into an extremely uncertain time with the lockout and CBA negotiations looming.

tigers.headline: A final look at the Detroit Tigers non-tender candidates
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers president of baseball operations Scott Harris watches practice during spring training at TigerTown in Lakeland, Fla. on Friday, Feb. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Friday, November 20 is the non-tender deadline for all arbitration eligible players. By 5:00 p.m. ET, every pre-arbitration and arbitration eligible player must be tendered a contract by their respective teams. Arb eligible players may ultimately turn down the offer and renegotiate or go to an arbitration hearing, typically in February though who knows this year, to decide their 2027 salary, but teams must tender them a contract by the deadline or they immediately become free agents without having to go through waivers. Typically, avoiding waivers is what non-tenders are for, allowing teams to try and negotiate a minor league deal rather than simply designating the player for assignment and giving the rest of the league a crack at them.

Often, players who aren’t going to be tendered a contract are just designated for assignment at the deadline to finalize the 40-man roster in advance of December’s Rule 5 draft. That deadline passed on Tuesday, and saw the Tigers trade infield prospect Jace Jung to the Los Angeles Angels for cash considerations to open one spot. Shortstop Trey Sweeney, outfielder Matt Vierling, and left-handed pitching prospect Jake Miller were all DFA’d off the 40-man roster as well. They’ll be non-tendered in the meantime. Free agent acquisition Emilio Pagán, along with prospects Josue Briceño, Max Anderson, and Peyton Graham were all added to the 40-man roster at that point, and the roster now stands at 40 players.

Here are the Tigers arbitration eligible players for 2027, their ages and service time, along with their 2026 salary and finally MLB Trade Rumors arbitration estimates.

Will Vest- Age 31 (5.100 years): $3.950MM —>$4.4MM

Zach McKinstry- Age 31 (5.099 years): $4.2MM —> $5MM

Riley Greene- Age 26 (4.110 years): $5.0MM —>$9.3MM

Spencer Torkelson- Age 27 (4.076 years): $4.075MM —>$7.7M

Kerry Carpenter-Age 29 (4.057 years): $3.275MM —>$4.1MM

Tyler Holton- Age 30 (4.047 years): $1.575MM —>$2.4MM

Beau Brieske- Age 28 (4.007 years): $1.157MM —>$1.5MM

Reese Olson- Age 27 (3.123 years): $818,100 —>$1.5MM

Wenceel Pérez- Age 26 (3.000 years): $803,400 —>$1.4 MM

Parker Meadows- Age 26 (2.169 years): $805,300 —>$1MM

Teams that weren’t going to offer their arbitration eligible players a contract often genearlly, but not always, would have just DFA’d them back on Tuesday to clear space for their additions. On the other hand, waiting does give a few extra days to look through the newly available players for potential upgrades, or to perhaps work out a trade of their own arbitration eligible player instead of just releasing the player outright. Typically this involves a veteran player who underperformed but still has value, but is also due a sizable raise in arbitration. The Tigers don’t really a player who fits that description, though Spencer Torkelson is arguably in that camp, so expect Friday to be pretty quiet unless they’re actively working to trade away one of the players above. Sweeney and Vierling haven’t been claimed as of yet, and so the Tigers will have them on their non-tender list, but they probably won’t have much company.

We’ve wondered if the Tigers might try to deal someone like Spencer Torkelson or Kerry Carpenter for minor league pitching depth as they get a bit more expensive, but there’s nothing to suggest that a trade is coming and both players value is at a low point. Neither is making that much, though Torkelson’s projected $7.7 million is starting to get a little close to his actual projected value for 2027. However, Scott Harris has continued to speak highly of Torkelson as a piece of the Tigers’ offense, so we’ll assume he’ll be tendered a contract.

Carpenter is still going to be quite cheap, although his status after the past two seasons is pretty uncertain. The injury history and declining recent production makes it unlikely that many teams will be inquiring about the 29-year-old outfielder, though his projected raise to $4.1 million is still quite inexpensive if he can get healthy and start turning things around at the plate. On the other hand, he’s a well liked player in the Tigers’ organization, and if teams aren’t offering anything in trade, non-tendering him would allow him to become a free agent and have some say in choosing his future home rather than exposing him to waivers via a DFA. The same could be true of fellow outfielders Wenceel Pérez and Parker Meadows, but that duo is still inexpensive and young enough that the Tigers will probably stick with them for now.

Utilityman Zach McKinstry isn’t projected for much of a raise, and his jack of all trades stylings help fill in gaps on the Tigers roster. Still, after a rough year at the plate he’s certainly a possible candidate to be non-tendered too, just as Andy Ibáñez was last year. It’s hard to imagine the Tigers managing to trade him for anything they need. Still, he could be tendered a contract to keep him under club control and then released later if the Tigers sign another free agent or claim a player off waivers before the season begins. At age 31, with minimal trade value, non-tendering him would at least allow him some control over his 2027 landing spot as well.

Finally, while the Tigers will keep Will Vest, right-hander Beau Brieske is out of options and is a pretty good non-tender candidate as well. The right-hander has spent the past two seasons dealing with shoulder issues. He briefly returned in May of 2026 but was roughed up. Still, he eventually got his legs under him and posted a 3.04 ERA and a 3.48 FIP from June 10 until the end of the season. With relief help at a premium, the Tigers might decide to keep him, but ideally they’d just non-tender him now and re-sign him to a minor league deal before the lockout begins. They could still pay him to accept this and stash him in Triple-A to begin the year. Of course, in that case Brieske could just choose to go elsewhere, but it’s not as though his services will be in high demand.

Last year the Tigers non-tendered Ibáñez and six pitchers, but the 40-man roster situation was pretty crowded due to pitcher injuries throughout the season. Tanner Rainey, Sean Guenther, Dugan Darnell, Jason Foley, Jack Little, and Tyler Mattison were all designated for assignment at the 40-man roster last year, and then ultimately non-tendered as well. Rainey, Little, and Mattison all ultimately accepted minor league deals with the Tigers.

The non-tender deadline is always the final Friday before Thanksgiving, per the 2022-2026 collective bargaining agreement. Generally, there isn’t a whole lot of big news, but occasionally a trade or two will go through in advance of the deadline, or there will be a surprise non-tender candidate. With the trade market perking up this week, there’s at least a chance that the Tigers make a small trade and non-tender a player or two to clear space for future free agent signings. Really the interest today is whether teams come to agreements with players quickly, and how the looming CBA fight might affect players’ willingness to actually sign a tendered contract now rather than waiting for an arbitration hearing under a new agreement.

tigers.headline: Dillon Dingler, Kevin McGonigle, and Riley Greene win Silver Slugger awards
tigers.body:
Aug 15, 2025; Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA; Detroit Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler (13) and left fielder Riley Greene (31) celebrate the win over the Minnesota Twins at Target Field. Mandatory Credit: Bruce Kluckhohn-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Awards season is finally concluding for the 2026 season, and tonight the Silver Slugger awards were announced. The award recognizes the best offensive player at each position in both leagues, and the Tigers took home three of them on the night. Riley Greene won a Silver Slugger among AL outfielders, while Kevin McGonigle took home his first in the utility category. Catcher Dillon Dingler also took home his first Silver Slugger as the top hitting catcher in the American League.

The 26-year-old Greene took home his second straight Silver Slugger with a campaign that featured 21 homers in 140 games, with a slash line of .280/.370/.474 on the year. His 136 wRC+ was the highest of his career, and he was able to trim strikeouts and add walks from his 2025 production for a better all around performance at the plate. With two years remaining until free agency, questions have started to swirl around the Tigers long-term plans for Greene, but there has been no public acknowledgement of interest in an extension from either party. His status throughout 2027 will be interesting in that light, but Greene has established himself as one of the top slugging outfielders in the game even as his defensive performance has slipped each of the past two seasons.

As for Dingler, the 28-year-old catcher looked like a sure fire MVP candidate for much of his second full season in the major leagues. Already the best all-around defensive catcher in baseball, Dingler hit 27 home runs with a .243/.302/.446 slash line, good for a 107 wRC+ on the year. By the end of July, Dingler already had 23 home runs with a .269/.333/.520 slash line, good for a 136 wRC+, but between catching most games and DH-ing a lot due to the Tigers need for offense, he crashed to Earth in August and September. Hopefully the Tigers can get him off his feet a little more in 2027 and get something closer to that first half performance all season long.

As for McGonigle, not much needs be said. The AL Rookie of the Year put together one of the best campaigns from a 21-year-old in league history. He hit 18 home runs a posted a 129 wRC+ with a slash line of .278/.376/.430 on the year. He takes home the Silver Slugger in the utility category after splitting his time pretty equally between shortstop and third base, which is all the more impressive from a rookie trying to adapt to the big leagues.

No team racked up more Silver Slugger awards in either league this season. The last time the Detroit Tigers had three in a year was back in 1987, when Alan Trammell, Lou Whitaker, and Matt Nokes all won the award.

Congratulations to Riley Greene, Kevin McGonigle, and Dillon Dingler, your Tigers’ Silver Slugger award winners for 2026.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign Emilio Pagán, protect three players from the Rule 5 draft
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers outfielder Matt Vierling walks off the field after practice during spring training at TigerTown in Lakeland, Fla. on Monday, Feb. 19, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Tigers have made their moves to finalize the 40-man roster in advance of Friday’s non-tender deadline and to protect prospects from the Rule 5 draft. First, they announced the official signing of reliever Emilio Pagán on an $11.5 million deal that has an extra million in incentives based on innings pitched attached. They added three prospects, C/1B Josue Briceño, INF Peyton Graham, and INF Max Anderson to the 40-man roster. To clear four spots, OF Matt Vierling, LHP Jake Miller, 1B/2B Jace Jung, and SS Trey Sweeney were all designated for assignment.

We expected that Jung and Sweeney were on the chopping block. The former couldn’t crack the Tigers roster this season despite the huge injury issues they had in the first half of the season. Sweeney just hasn’t been able to get the bat going since the Tigers traded for him in 2024, and he missed the whole season due to shoulder surgery. Jung needs a new home where perhaps he can get some shots at the big leagues again. Sweeney is a solid candidate to sign a minor league deal if the Tigers are interested in keeping him for depth and seeing how he looks once he’s fully rehabilitated.

Vierling was the obvious choice among the outfielders on the cut line. After solid work in 2023-2024, Vierling hasn’t been able to stay on the field, and he hasn’t hit when he has been healthy. Now 30 years old, the veteran outfielder is running out of time to get his career back on track, and with plenty of depth outfield options in the organization, he was certainly expendable now.

Jake Miller is a talented lefty with excellent command and one of my favorite upper minors pitching prospects in the system. However, he’s spent the last two years battling lower back and hip problems and had double labrum surgery 13 months ago to correct the issues. He was only able to get back on the mound briefly this season and then went back on the injured list for the rest of the year. Hopefully they can sign Miller back on a minor league deal. A team might take a shot on him, but there’s a fair chance he sneaks through the Rule 5 draft with his medical status so uncertain. Either way, the Tigers probably feel like they’re in good shape for lefties and could take that chance.

Because those three are injured, they cannot be outrighted to Triple-A Toledo the way Jung could, so the Tigers will have to non-tender them on Friday, and then sign them on minor league deals if they want to keep them and if the players agree.

Adding Briceño and Anderson was obvious. Both will be looked to as part-time contributors to the offense next season as they get their first cracks at the major leagues. Less so is the addition of infielder Peyton Graham. The 25-year-old long-time shortstop has struggled to add the muscle we hoped he could on draft day. Even so, he’s turned into a solid hitter who gets on base and puts his plus speed to work. He and Seth Stephenson took advantage of the one disengagement rule in the Eastern League this season and tied for the lead in stolen bases with 66.

I was a big fan of Graham’s on draft day and have hung in their with him to a degree as his stock has fallen. While I always forecast him as a probable late bloomer with the bat, the thing that has really hurt his stock the past two years has been the lack of major improvements at the shortstop position. Graham has the speed and the arm strength to play well there, but continues to be too error prone with a bad habit of throwing the ball away when on the run or pressed for time. He has played second base and even some center field, and presumably the plan is to move him more fully into utility player territory. He’s shown some ability to play center field, and the Tigers can use that versatility in a right-handed bat.

Graham has some power too, but his long swing path has made it tougher on him to drive the ball to the pull side as he’s faced tougher pitching. Still, he hit .290 with a whopping .397 on-base percentage this year, with modest power production and nine homers overall. Graham dealt with a lot of minor, nagging injuries early in his pro career, so let’s hope he really is a late bloomer.

The Tigers roster now stands at 40 players, so any other free agent moves will require a corresponding move.
